reality is we have a Senate. There are a lot of things that I do not care for. There are a lot of things the government does that I do not care for, but we have to live with these things. We have to live with the Senate. So, let us give the Senate an opportunity to prove itself. It has the constitutional authority to kill legislation. That is reality. I might not like it, I might not endorse it, I might not support it, but that is reality.
My leader asked the Senate to do something responsible for once and rather than simply review legislation, hundreds and thousands of pieces of it, do something that the people of Canada want it to do as senators, and defeat the goods and services tax. It failed to do that. It is not doing that. It gives no indication that it has any intention of listening to the people of Canada. That is why, today, we bring forward this motion which states we should not provide funding to allow the Senate to operate any longer. In other words, not give it the $27-plus million they require to carry on.
This would essentially abolish the Senate. Nelson Riis today, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, is putting forward this initiative to abolish the Senate. We cannot be any clearer than that in terms of how we feel when it comes to this particular Senate and the way it operates. The reality is that it exists and I am providing an opportunity for my friend, the government House Leader, and for the government, to do the right thing and not concur in this motion to provide operating funds to allow the other place an opportunity to continue for another fiscal year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to say that I was amazed in listening to the hon. member for Kamloops would be putting it mildly. I can only say how glad I am he has come back to the Chamber. I know he was away Monday when the motion his party put forward was debated. I looked forward to his participation in that debate.
The hon. member is now saying he wants to abolish the Senate. He now says that is party policy. Yet, on May 10 in the House, he told us the NDP policy had changed. He made an announcement that apparently at the December convention the NDP decided to scrap the policy of abolition. The hon. member for Edmonton East apparently had not grasped that fact. That became obvious on Monday. There may be dissension in the NDP about what their policy really is. Some seem to
think it is still abolition, some say it is not. It is a personal view of his that abolition is still-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is a personal view.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is a personal sort of view.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The government House leader says it is a personal sort of view. But, somehow, we do not know what NDP policy is on this.
You never do.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
On the one hand they say "we want to abolish the Senate". Some of the members seem to think that. Apparently their official policy is to look at other options. That is what the hon. member for Kamloops said on May 10. On Monday they were saying how the Senate really was very important and should exercise its constitutional rights and block government bills willy-nilly. It was right there in the motion.
I am sorry the hon. member for Kamloops did not participate in that debate because I am sure he would have supported that motion. It was his party's official position. Or, perhaps the hon. member Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca went off on his own and dumped this motion on the Order Paper by mistake on Friday afternoon. We do not know what happened, but I wish the hon. member for Kamloops had clarified that for us in his remarks on the Senate. We would appreciate hearing his views. Nevertheless, having moved this motion on Monday saying that it supports the Senate, today we now have the hon. member for Kamloops trying to take away the Senate's money so it cannot do what the NDP wanted it to do on Monday.
What is the NDP position? What is the hon. member for Kamloops really saying? Are some of the members of the NDP in favour of abolition and others not? Do some think the Senate should block this legislation and some not, or is he simply playing a game and trying to blame the Liberal Party for the passage of this bad tax that this Tory government has introduced? Is that what he is really trying to do? If so, does the New Democratic Party, being a party of principle, not think that politics is a naughty thing to do and it should not be engaging in such silliness?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, imagine politics in the House of Commons. What is going to happen next, politics in the Parliament of Canada? I guess I have to admit that, from time to time, politics does rear its lovely head in here.
June 6, 1990

In response to my friend, I have two points. Yes, I was trying to point out the fact that the Liberals in the Senate are passing the GST. I must confess to that. They are passing the GST, just like the Conservatives in the House of Commons passed the GST. To clarify for my hon. friend, the motion on Monday read as follows:
That a message be sent to the Senate reminding the Senate that it has the constitutional right and the power to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons.
Anybody who understands how Parliament works would agree that the Senate has the authority to do just that, so that is a given. It is just a reminder, I suppose, to my hon. friend that that is the reality of our parliamentary system, that the Senate has the power and the authority to defeat any bill.
All we were asking on Monday was that the Senate do what we would expect it to do, in terms of listening to the people of Canada and defeat the bill. The Senate has failed to do that. We have given it ample time to indicate if it intends to defeat the goods and services tax, but the Senate obviously does not. The Liberals in the Senate plan, as they already have voted in favour of the tax once in the Senate, to take a little bit of time but eventually pass it one way or the other. Probably a lot of people will be sick on that day, or away or whatever and their incentive plan will not work to bring in the senators. Eventually they will muster up a majority and probably pass it on division so it will not be clear who it was who supported it, but it will pass the Senate.
To answer my hon. friend's question: What is the NDP's position in terms of the Senate? I will read, specifically, from party policy, because I think my hon. friend asked a very important question. As far as the Parliament of Canada is concerned, it states that "The NDP will continue to fight for further changes, including the abolition of the Senate". As of the last party convention in 1989, Motion 30 reads, "and that the proposed committee on the Canadian Constitution examine options to promote better regional representation in the Parliament of Canada including, but not limited to, proportional representation, an elected Senate, a House of the provinces and territories, as well as the abolition of the Senate", in other words, a number of options.
Supply
All I can say is that the NDP has been consistent. We do not change our policy by the day. We develop our policy at the grass roots at party conventions and we support that. What we are doing is completely and totally consistent with party policy; it is totally consistent with initiatives that we have taken on Friday of last week, on Monday of this week and certainly today when we have asked for the abolition of the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to have an opportunity to make a few remarks in this debate. I have given a great deal of consideration as to how I might usefully contribute to the discussion. However, after listening to my hon. friend opposite, the hon. member for Kamloops, I must confess I am left a little bit confused as to exactly where the New Democratic Party stands with respect to the subject of democracy. If I understand correctly, what I have just heard the hon. member calling for is the other place to defeat legislation that, in the case of the GST, has been approved by this House. He is calling for the other place, the non-elected other place, to defeat that legislation and I find that a remarkable bit of confusion.
The hon. member says that that defeat should take place because of democracy, I believe that was the term; that the will of the people should prevail. I have lived with the understanding, perhaps it is a delusion, that the way we practise democracy in this country is that every so often Parliament is dissolved and we have an election and the people make their choices. It is, I believe, what is referred to as a representative democracy. Both in 1988 and in 1984 the people of Canada made their choice and gave an overwhelming mandate to this government to govern the country. Indeed, during the course of doing so, the government, through its elected representatives in the House of Commons, reflecting the perceptions of the will of the people, brings forth legislation that addresses the serious problems of this country and attempts to prepare Canada to move into the 21st century.
That is precisely what this government has been doing and has done in introducing the GST. My goodness gracious, changes in taxes are not popular things but sometimes they are necessary in a democratic country. We need a government that has the courage, the integrity, the honesty and a mandate from the people to get on with the business of the nation. I hear my hon. friend opposite suggesting that a non-elected body

June 6, 1990
Supply
should stop the will of the people, the will of the people as freely expressed in a democratic way at the polls.
We have had, in my opinion, an absolute travesty of democracy for the last several months in this country as we have seen the other place not once, not twice, but three times flaunt the will of the elected people of this country in passage of Bill C-21. This bill is a long overdue revamping of the unemployment insurance system in this country, a bill that is in fact going to take our unemployment insurance from being a passive approach to making it an active approach. Among other things, it is going to make changes that are tremendously beneficial to the people of this country.
Thinking in terms of my own South Shore riding in southern Nova Scotia, I think of the crisis that we are facing right now because of the downturn in the Atlantic fishery. I think of the fact that fish plants are closing far more frequently than we might want.
Thanks to the fact that C-21 is not in place, those people now have to work 20 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance. If they would get that bill through, the number of weeks required to qualify for unemployment insurance would be down where it should be. Seasonal workers like fish plant workers would benefit because the repeater provision of the unemployment insurance system would be removed. Yet the other place, ignoring democracy, has refused to pass that legislation. That is something which should be a matter of grave concern to Canadians.
We have now passed Bill C-43 dealing with the contentious issue of abortion. That has caused anguish to Canadians from coast to coast in this country. What are the senators saying? They are not sure what they are going to do about Bill C-43. Perhaps they will hold public hearings on the subject. Goodness, gracious, is there anything left to be said on that particular subject and can we not get on with the governance of this country?
I must not allow myself to get waylaid by the confusion as to what democracy is or is not in the minds of what is called euphemistically the New Democratic Party. I must get on with my own comments about the other place. I happen to think it is a tragedy that the other place has strayed from what it was supposed to be. If we think back 125 years to the origins of our country, and we think of
the concept that existed at that time, of modelling a separate chamber, a chamber, if one reads the confederation debates, one sees was intended to provide what is referred to as a sober second thought. One does not know exactly what the state of sobriety that always might have existed in that or any other place, but nevertheless, the idea was that you had the elected people who essentially were charged with the responsibility of legislating for and governing the country, but you had this second body that would provide a second look that could enhance and contribute to the legislative process in Canada.
The idea was that very distinguished Canadians would be identified and asked to serve in that other place and that it would be a showcase of outstanding Canadians. I was perusing the latest issue of, I forget what it is called, something like the parliamentary guide. It gives little biographies of all the members of this Chamber and the other. I could not help but think to myself that indeed, sitting in that other place are a number of very distinguished Canadians; people who hold the Order of Canada and people who represent various vocations and professions in this country. I was thinking to myself what a tragedy it is the way that place has been abused, the way the credibility of that place, as an institution that could contribute with great value to this country, is being destroyed in the minds of Canadians.
Indeed, it is being destroyed in the minds of all people who believe in the democratic process and who believe that representative parliamentary government is the basis of democracy as we approach the end of this century.
Instead, what we have is gamesmanship being played by people of the Liberal Party who once sat in this place. I think of the distinguished gentleman who for many years represented my province in this place and now sits in the other chamber as Leader of the Opposition. I cannot help but wonder what he would have said when he sat here as House leader or Deputy Prime Minister. What would he have said if the opposition in the other place had done with his legislation what he is now doing with legislation that has been brought in after careful consideration to benefit Canadians from coast to coast? What a tragedy.
What has it come to? Where is it leading? In this country for the last several weeks, and in particular for the last three or four days, we have seen intensive discussion on the subject of Senate reform. We should not need Senate reform. The Senate is not what it is supposed to be. The people there are distinguished Canadians who do not recognize their proper role.
As my hon. friend from Kamloops said, legally and technically the Senate has the right to block legislation here. We also have convention. I am mindful of 1981 and 1982 when constitutional changes, on which there was failure to receive accord of all the Premiers of the country, were being proposed. Contraiy to the convention of this country, the government proceeded without the support of the province of Quebec in implementing the constitutional changes of 1982. This is, perhaps, one of the main reasons that we find ourselves in the state in which this country has been for the last few months.
Convention allowed Quebec to oppose that constitution. Propriety and wisdom would have said: "You do not do it until you get everybody to come together." We now have the same attitude, value and ethic being used in the other place, not surprisingly, by the very same people who had no more respect for propriety and convention when they sat over here than evidently they have in the other place today. In my judgment, that is a most regrettable thing.
The outcome of all of this, in my opinion, could be that increasing numbers of Canadians will end up drawing the same conclusion as the conclusion my hon. friend from Kamloops suggested. In fact, it is the position of his party, that is, that the Senate should be abolished.
Clearly, if the Senate is unable to perform the valuable role it can play for this country and if the role of the Senate de facto is going to be to disrupt the carrying on of democracy, then indeed there is no alternative except to get rid of it. I, for one, think that would be a most regrettable state of affairs if that happened.
Instead, I would rather see the other place and the leadership of the Liberal Party in the other place recognize the difference between propriety and abuse of position. I would rather have it recognize the will of a democratically elected government in this country with
Supply
the courage to lead and the common sense to get on with what the needs of Canada are for the 21st century. Then, Canadians would be well served. Indeed, all members of this House would be most enthusiastic in supporting measures that will provide the financial basis for them to operate in the other place.
I do not want to transgress for too lengthy a period of time on the House, but I will say in conclusion that I urge all members of the House, and in particular I urge all members of the Liberal Party in the House to go to their colleagues up the hall and tell them that it is time they had respect for the democratic process of the country. It is time they had respect for propriety and convention, so that the country can get on with its own business as it should. Canadians would have confidence in parliamentarians at both ends of this hall, as should be the case.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a very brief comment.
I listened with great intensity and interest to the hon. member from South Shore. I am sure what he had to say was technically correct, but he glossed over a few points which I think I should certainly raise.
Whether it is in defence of the Senate or not, my particular issue is with some of the comments he made on Bill C-21, which is an issue of some concern to those of us on this side of the House and particularly those of us from the Atlantic region.
My hon. friend talked about the extension beyond the usual 10 or 12 weeks, whatever it is in the particular UIC region that has been charted out, up to as high as 20 weeks in my riding from 10 to 14 weeks. I am sure anybody watching this debate on television would have been very conscious of the comment that was made by the hon. member for South Shore.
Just to refresh his memory, Mr. Speaker, unemployment insurance was brought into this country about 50 years ago by the Liberal Party as a protection for those who did not have jobs and could not find jobs in tough times so that they would not be hungry.
It was a practice by both governments since 1977 to pass what was called a variable entrance requirement. This, in effect, recognized the areas of higher unemployment, reduced qualifying time, and gave extended

June 6, 1990
Supply
periods of benefit in accordance with the requirements and in direct relationship to the rate of unemployment.
This happened every year since 1977 on an annual basis and almost as a matter of course and, I believe I am correct in saying, almost without debate, until Bill C-21 was introduced in this House last April by the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration, debated in the House of Commons and, indeed, debated across the country.
Bill C-21 included the variable entrance requirement. Without using unparliamentary language I think it is safe to say that Bill C-21 was held hostage, as was indeed the variable entrance requirement, to the whole procedure. In other words, the drill was if you do not pass C-21 you will be punished and you will not get the variable entrance requirement.
The other place being discussed here in very negative terms, the place of second sober thought, had the wisdom, foresight, integrity, and courage just before Christmas last year, in fact moments before this House adjourned for the Christmas break, to reintroduce Bill S-12. This was the variable entrance requirement, the very measure that the hon. member talked about so despicably and which he voted against along with his other members.
How can he possibly blame the Senate for that? In fact, I hope he will remember that he voted against this when we break during the summer because people will remember.
I just want to wrap this up by saying we talk about democracy. A great man, Abraham Lincoln, talked about democracy as being "by the people, of the people, and for the people".
Well, I have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, 300 committee items, various people, teams, individuals, appeared before groups of the Commons committee and the Senate committee when they went across the country. Ninety-five per cent of those disagreed with Bill C-21 and, indeed, 90 per cent were very much against it.
That may be democracy "of the people" but I do not think it is "by the people" and it certainly is not "for the people".

Mr. Speaker, I am more than pleased to respond to my hon. friend though I must confess that I
think the House has seen an absolutely extraordinary thing happen here. We have invoked the name and the distinguished Gettysburg Address of Abraham Lincoln, the sixteenth President of the United States, to defend the absolute abrogation of propriety and democratic principles by the people up the hall.
My hon. friend knows perfectly well that he speaks with his tongue in his cheek when he says what he has just said in this place with respect to Bill C-21 and the variable entrance requirement. It is interesting.
I call to his attention what happened in this very Chamber in 1977 when Bill C-27 was moved by the previous government. It was a bill not dissimilar in much of its intent to Bill C-21. It brought in a number of changes. In fact it was the one that introduced for the first time the variable entrance requirement.
It brought in a number of other similar changes. It was hotly debated in this Chamber. In fact the government of that day, which by the way was a government formed by the same people who now sit on the other side of the floor in this Chamber, brought in time allocation to impose that bill on this House at that time.
I wonder what they would have thought if the people down the hall had said: "We are going to take our time with this piece of legislation". Interestingly enough, many of those same principles were debated before that bill had been put through this place with time allocation. What happened to that bill when it got down the hall? The bill was introduced on August 2, 1977 and reported without amendment the following day, August 3, 1977. What of the principles in the other place? The same people had the majority in that place. It is interesting to check the record.
We see that the following year Bill C-14 was introduced in this place dealing with the subject of unemployment insurance and a number of very contentious issues including, I might point out, that it would result in a saving of $885 million in UI benefits, a remarkable achievement. What happened to that bill? That bill was similarly dealt with in a very contentious manner in this place. What happened? Were they worried about it in the other place? It passed through the other place and received Royal Assent in one day, on December 22,1978.

Yet if my hon. friend would check the record, and I invite him to do so, it is interesting to note that as they went on their grand tour of Canada to hear witnesses they heard from 54 of the same witnesses who appeared before the C-21 legislative committee of this House.
While I enjoy my friend's eloquence, as always, I am not sure exactly what his question was. His question had to do with a bill originating in the other place.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to enter the debate this afternoon, especially before the member for South Shore explodes.
For people who are watching today on television and for those in the gallery, the debate that we are seeing among the Liberals, the Conservatives, and the New Democrats is interesting. The debate is on where these various parties stand on the question of the Senate.
The New Democratic Party's House leader, the hon. member for Kamloops, made it very clear in reading our party's policy from our recent convention in Winnipeg, at which we elected our new leader, the member for Yukon, that the New Democratic Party has always had a

June 6, 1990
Supply
strategic and forward thinking policy when it comes to the Senate.
Why do I say that, or why can I say that? The reason I can say that is that we do not have the hidebound approach to dealing with the Senate of our friends in the Liberal and Conservative parties. Let us take a look at history. Let us look at the historic debate that we are having today, that we had as well on Monday, and that the First Ministers are having down the street today.
We all know the history of the Senate. All those who go through school and university have probably written at least one essay on the Senate and how it should be abolished. It represented the classes with property. It gives a sober second look at legislation from the House of Commons, from the commoners. Property was a requirement to be appointed to that place. I believe, if I have my history right that, the right hon. member for Yellowhead was the Prime Minister who appointed one of his friends to the Senate who had to buy a condominium in Ottawa in order to be eligible to accept his appointment to the Senate.
I recall debate in the House at one time when the current Prime Minister asked in this House the then Leader of the Opposition, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, if he would agree on the spot, that day, to legislation to abolish the Senate. We agreed. Our leader, Mr. Broadbent, the former member for Oshawa, agreed with the Tories that day that the Senate should be abolished then and there.
However who was it, which party was it that refused the necessary consent to abolish the Senate that day? You guessed right, Mr. Speaker. It was the Liberals again. Why?
It is pretty clear from the debate today and the debate we have heard in the House, particularly over the goods and services tax, that the Liberals are in favour of preserving the Senate as much as the Conservatives are. Of course the debate around that has been around the goods and services tax.
It was revealing when our House leader just mentioned to this House that in fact Liberal senators of the Liberal dominated Senate have actually now given second reading to the goods and services tax legislation. It is on its way to becoming law. It is becoming law with the
co-operation and assistance of the Conservatives in the House of Commons and the Liberals in the Senate.
It is clear from the attitude exhibited in the House by the Liberals that they feel confident that they are going to walk into office in the next election, just as the Conservatives feel so confident that they will be able to pull it off at the last minute and get re-elected. However the Liberals want to try and have it as many different ways as they can. When that legislation goes through- and all Canadians know the kind of tax grab the goods and services tax is-the Liberal Party of Canada cannot wait to get its hands on that money.
We know as well that even the leadership candidates for the Liberal Party are not clear on where they stand on the goods and services tax. We have had a couple of alternatives put forward from the Liberals. There has been the flat tax proposal.
The single tax.

The flat earth proposal. The New Democrats have presented clear and consistent policies when it comes to alternatives to tax policy in this country.
Today we are giving the Liberals and the Conservatives the opportunity in this House to join with the first ministers in starting to take a look at what we should do with the Senate.
Monday was an historic day. We said in our policy that it is a tool that can be used. We said: "If you are so opposed to the GST then stop the legislation now. Use your power now to do that".
What did they do? We know what is happening with the Liberals senators and the GST. They are trying to
pass it.
The motion today gives a chance to government members to send a clear signal to the Liberal senators: "Stop delaying our legislation. We have a right to pass it". The Conservative members should vote for our motion, thereby doing in the Senate which can then go along and pass the legislation.
They can give it a try. We will oppose it in this House as we always have. Here is the chance for the Conservatives to send a very clear signal to the Senate of Canada to understand the importance of the kind of legislation it

will or will not support. I think that is the importance of this motion today.
Let us look at what the Senate does. It cost taxpayers $40 million a year for that unelected body, our senators. They work Tuesday through to Thursday. They have an 800 number so that Canadians can give them a call.
In my province, in my area, if we closed down the Senate for five years we would come close to having enough money finally to plant some trees. I think we could do more good for British Columbia and our environment by planting some trees rather than keeping the Senate going for a couple more years when who knows what it is doing.
The motion put forward by our House leader, the member for Kamloops, is part of a strategic policy platform. It is a forward thinking policy that our party has had, a policy which developed out of our convention in Winnipeg. We foresaw the debate that is going on now with the First Ministers with respect to how to change the Senate. Is it going to be changed or abolished? What are we going to do with the Senate? We are waiting just as all members and all Canadians are, to see what the first ministers come up with on the Senate.
We do not know what is going on, of course. It is a closed shop debate right now. I think we would all be interested to see exactly what the future of this country is going to be.
I wonder if the members of the Conservative Party in this House really know that their Prime Minister is saying down the street with the First Ministers. I wonder if they know what the Prime Minister is talking about when it comes to the Senate. Probably not. We have already heard some interventions by members to get in there and state their views, which is what all Canadians are arguing for.
These are historic days for the Senate in terms of its reform or its abolition. As well, I think that the motion that we have brought forward here today sends out a clear signal. My guess is that the Conservatives will probably be supporting our motion today because they want to send a clear signal to the Liberal-dominated Senate as well. I think we will have some support from the Conservatives with our motion so that we can send that signal.

In conclusion, politicians being what they are in their various chambers-and I suppose we and the Senate are not alone, and nor are other legislative chambers-sometimes cause Canadians to wonder about what it is we are doing. The latest example will become a new symbol. It is a $153 symbol just for showing up for work, on top of your normal pay because you show up for work.
The next button that will be a best seller in Canada will be a button showing $153 with a red line through it. It will become a symbol of exactly where we are with the Senate. Canadians are going to be outraged by that particular measure. They are going to be outraged by senators who now suggest that they need another $153 a day just to show up for work.
As the member for Kamloops said, maybe we will actually have a couple of extra days when senators will show up in Ottawa. Planes will be full of senators rushing back to Ottawa to try and collect their $153 a day. It has become an important symbol.
Before I sit down, and to put that symbol into meaning, I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting the sum of $27,605,000
and replacing it with the sum of $27,604,847.
That motion symbolizes that $153 the senators now want to pay themselves.

They actually think it is a beneficial tax, one that will provide viability and fiscal capability for Canada for many years in the future. You might say in that respect that they agree entirely with the government party that the GST is basically an appropriate instrument of taxation and one which they really in fact support despite their posture in the House of Commons, and that it will be approved in the Senate.
I gather that is the point that the New Democratic Party is making. Of course, on the other hand it is continuing its unrealistic opposition to the Senate. As the member for Kamloops said, he has to deal with reality. I never thought I would hear a socialist say that they would have to deal with reality, but the reality is that the Senate is there, and members of the New Democratic Party recognize that. They have made this arcane appeal, knowing that the appeal is going to be denied and that the GST is going to be approved. It is simply to show that the Liberal Party in fact supports the GST.
Could I ask the member this? Have I understood correctly the position of the New Democratic Party?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that the member's son is out planting trees in the great north of British Columbia. A number of other members have sons and daughters doing just that. We are glad they are making that contribution to the country.
The hon. member got part of the message right, not the whole of it. We are saying in this debate, as we have throughout all of the debate on the goods and services tax that, in the member's words, the Liberal Party has been less than honest about its real intentions on the goods and services tax.
It has already passed second reading the Senate, as you know, Mr. Speaker. I think most Canadians will be surprised to hear that that has actually happened.
Yes, part of the message in the debate we are having today is about the honesty of the Liberal Party on the GST.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short question for my friend.
During his speech he made the comment that we sometimes do things in this House that Canadians must
June 6, 1990

wonder about. I realize that it is the New Democratic Party's opposition day. But, as the member from Halifax mentioned earlier, by constitution we must at this point in time let the Senate carry on. I am not going to get into whether I am for or against the Senate at this moment, but I will tell hon. members what really irritates me. By the way, the Senate has not passed the GST. It is going to committee now. Do not mislead the people of Canada by saying that the Senate has rubber-stamped or passed the GST. But that is not the point I want to make.
The point I want to make is that I really think that we in this House today must look like idiots. Interest rates are going through the moon. There is a housing crisis. We should be using this place to focus on the real problems that exist in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate some of what the member for Broadview-Greenwood has had to say. I think we all know what is going on in the Liberal Party now. I guess some of us know, or we read between the lines. The member has made some sincere attempts to convince his leadership candidates of some of his proposals and ideas. I would say that that is probably good. Most of the leadership candidates have been a little loosey-goosey when it comes to saying exactly where they stand on some of their policies, particularly the GST.
I know my hon. friend has been pursuing one particular tax policy idea, to his credit. He is working hard at trying to convince his colleagues to adopt that approach and policy.
He expresses some chagrin about the debate in the House today. I would say very sincerely that from time to

time, as I said earlier and he agreed, that Houses such as ours, and others, do things or debate issues about which Canadians might wonder.
Mr. Speaker has been quite helpful for the people who watch our proceedings on television. From time to time he takes a second or two to explain exactly what we are doing.
What we are doing in the House is using opportunities to debate issues, which is what we are doing now. This is not a frivolous motion. The debate about the future of the Senate is as serious in this Chamber now as it is down the street where the First Ministers are having their say about the future of the Senate.
We are talking about a motion which concerns $27 million or $40 million a year. What will be even sillier is that some time tonight we are all going to say yea or nay to this vote. Mr. Speaker, I just want to ask my colleague a question. In his speech he made a number of comments about the position of leadership candidates of the Liberal Party and the Liberal Party itself on the GST. Several spokespersons for the Liberal Party have clearly indicated our opposition to a regressive tax. We know that the Senate is indicating very clearly that it will provide Canadians with an opportunity to review the tax, because there are many changes occurring in this tax, even since it was passed by this place. The Senate will be providing that forum for Canadians.
I have a specific question for my colleague. He has grave concern for positions and alternatives to the government proposal on GST. Both the Canadian Labour Congress and the New Democratic Party, in briefs presented to the Standing Committee on Finance of the House of Commons, indicated that they sought a royal commission and that there should be tax reform based on a royal commission. I wonder if my colleague would be kind enough to explain why the NDP puts forward the thesis that it has a position on the goods and services tax if it is asking the people of Canada to foot the expense

June 6, 1990

for a royal commission to find an alternative to the government proposal?

Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to respond to that question because it is an important one. I hope and trust that my reply will give an indication of just how seriously we have thought out the approach which we want to take to taxation policy in the country.
First, yes, we have made allegations about Liberal leadership candidates and how loosey-goosey they are when it comes to GST policy and other tax policies. They are playing politics and some of the front-runners do not want to be pinned down to one particular policy or another because then immediately positions are formed up. We all know in the House what that is all about. I guess it is about how sincere one is going to be and what about those frontrunners and exactly where are they going to stand. Our friends in the Liberal Party have tabled petition after petition calling on the Conservatives to stop and end the GST now.
Suddenly, the GST legislation is in the Senate. It has passed second reading and it is on to committee. Why are they not now urging and encouraging the Senate to stop the GST legislation right at this moment? There are some serious questions that people have raised about Liberal leadership candidates and whatever their strategy is when it comes to the goods and services tax.
The question from the member about a royal commission on tax policy is a good one. Our proposal is a package of 18 to 20 significant alternatives and suggested tax measures dealing with the goods and services tax. One of them is the call for a royal commission into taxation policy. Aside from, along with, and parallel to the tax measures that we are suggesting, it is important to bring in the Income Tax Act every now and then, put it up on the hoist and take a good look at it, quite like we are supposed to do with the Bank Act. We have reached a pivotal time for tax policy and a good close look at our taxation policy should be taken. We have suggested that it should be done through a royal commission. I think that is a credible and responsible approach to take and this would include our other tax policies, when it comes to alternatives to the goods and services tax.
Mr. Speaker, I was sitting here and minding my own business-
I don't believe that.
He was minding the nation's business.

I was minding my business. My friend, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood, pricked my conscience. I have great respect for him. He is a thoughtful member of Parliament, very thoughtful. He puts it all on one page. Any member of Parliament who can put all of his thoughts on one page, I respect.
He suggested that with the big issues facing the nation, Canadians must be wondering what we are doing in the House talking about the Senate and they must think we are crazy. He is absolutely right.
I want to tell him and all Canadians that Canadians right across this land who are not wealthy are absolutely shocked that an unelected group of people can sit over there and vote themselves a $153 a day. That is to show up. They still get their $62,000 a year along with their $10,000 tax-free allowance. They now get $153 a day tax free to show up. It is absolutely outrageous. Do you know that there are poor people in the country who live for a week on $153?
Of course, they need an incentive to show up for work. God knows they find very little time to show up. A $153-a-day incentive. Do people understand the estimates that we are voting today? I tell my hon. friend from Broadview-Greenwood to look at what I see in expenditure: $1,525,000 for the construction of committee rooms in the Senate.
This is a time when we are asking Canadians to tighten their belts. We are asking them to make sacrifices. We are asking them to pay taxes on taxes on taxes. When it is not the federal government reaching into their pockets, it is the provincial governments, the school boards, municipalities, or hydro commissions. Everybody is into their pockets.
Is this not important to Canadians? Already I have received phone calls in my riding office because people heard on the news that the Senators voted themselves $153 a day. To whom are the senators accountable?
I was invited into a school the other day to talk about government. Here is a question that young people posed
June 6, 1990

to me: What does one do to get into the Senate? There is a tough question. I really have to think about that one.
First, one has to go to St. Francis Xavier University or the same kindergarten as the Prime Minister. The only way to get into the Senate is to be a friend of people in high places. The Senate is a resting home for all those who have served the Conservative Party and Liberal Party well. The Senate has become a hiving ground for all the flicks, flacks, and hacks of both the Conservative Party and Liberal Party. That is how one gets into the Senate.
This Senate is not elected. Therefore, there is no accountability. Lo and behold, senators can actually vote themselves $153 tax-free.
That is for showing up.

That is the incentive. The other thing is this business of a $1.5 million to renovate the committee rooms. If they show up, Madam Speaker, there has to be committee rooms for them.
The other question that the young people raised was: What does a Senator do? I have never been able to answer that question in all the 17 years that I have been involved in federal politics. Quite frankly, I have never seen a real live senator. In fact, the other day the cleaning people were cleaning up, a senator was there and he keeled over. She said: "Oh God, he is dead." She ran out to get the head of the cleaning staff who said: "Don't worry. He has been dead for years. He has been sitting there." I do not know what a senator does. I really don't.
The Senate is supposed to be a Chamber of sober second thought.
Does the NDP want the Senate to hold up the GST? That was your policy yesterday.

We will get to that.
What we have is a second chamber, not elected, not accountable, and suddenly now revived. The Senate became the issue around which the future of Canada was to be decided. Can you believe this moribund place suddenly became the focus around which the future of the country would be decided. I cannot believe it.
Supply
I think our proposal is a very simple one. If the government supports the motion of the hon. member for Kamloops to eliminate the $47 million, voila, the problem is resolved. The government's headaches are finished. The solution is one of the hitches in the Meech Lake Accord is eliminated. Then, without a Senate, we can start to look at how to reform the House of Commons on a proportional representation basis. We can build into the elected chamber representation from the regions of the country, over and above the elected members.

You were doing well until a minute
ago.
No. If you follow me. I really-
The responsibility is over there at the railway station.

No, the responsibility is ours, right here. We are faced with an opportunity to resolve it.
I heard the government House leader the other day when Bill C-21 came back to the House. He made a speech in which he raled against the fact that the Senate was unaccountable and dominated by ex-Liberals who got a second coming over there and somehow are dictating policy for this House. I heard the government House leader say that.
They are still Liberal die-hards.

They are still Liberals, yes, in different clothing. But there they are over there. I heard the government House leader rale against the Senate because of what it did to Bill C-21.
The obvious solution to that problem is not to stack it with more Tory hacks to outvote the Liberal hacks. The solution to the problem is to cut the tree down. Go right to the roots and pull it out. Take it right out. That is the solution to the problem. We, today, have given the government an opportunity to solve its headache. Just think about it. If the government does what we ask it to do, it solves it here and it solves it across the street, in the Conference Centre. It is simple. No problem. No problem at all.
On the other hand, I am caught on the horns of a dilemma because I do recognize that a Senate can be useful. I know the problem. Even we sometimes would want a Senate where we could put all the people who give us particular problems in the NDR Then, the question logically extends, do we really need to have them here on the Hill? I do not think so. We could set them up in some sort of a hole and send the cheques. We

June 6, 1990
Supply
do not have to ring bells for them. We do not have to have people come knocking on our door here to invite us down. We do not have to have all of that stuff.
Now, what is rumoured from across the street? They want to increase the numbers in the Senate. They want to increase them.
There is an opportunity.

I am not preaching for a call, brother. I am quite happy here.
The problem that we are trying to help the government through is to pass the motion of the hon. member for Kamloops. I do not think that one can justify to the Canadian people an unelected body which thwarts the wishes of the elected members of Parliament. That is my position. That is our position. We believe that. But if the government persists in supporting the Senate and you want to keep it on our backs, then for heaven's sake we are going to use it against you. We are prepared and have put it in writing that if you want to cut it out, we will cut it out. But if you vote us down and foist this unelected group of party hacks and flacks on us, then we are going to use them. Why not? Absolutely, we should use them.
We socialists not only have principles, we are practical. And if you do not like those principles, we have others.
Madam Speaker, how can we be practical? I think the best way is to vote for the motion of the member for Kamloops and cut off their money supply.
The point is that this is our principle, to kill the Senate. We put a motion to do that. Now if the government votes it down as we know they will, I hope you vote with us and if we are defeated, so be it. We have achieved a policy that our party has established in convention, the elimination of the Senate.
We have not rescinded. In fact, Liberals and Conservatives constantly get together to support the other place, and we are practical. Until you defeat it we recognize that we have to use it. And we are going to use it against you. We are going to use the Senate as we are using it with the GST, to say to them: "If you are sincere Liberals, simply vote against the GST, defeat the GST, do not send it back".
Now a greater principle than that is the principle that there should be no unelected, unaccountable group of men and women sitting in the other place who deny the desires of the elected group. That's not democratic. In fact they not only deny the right of the elected body to pass legislation, but they turn around and impose more taxes on the people of Canada to the tune of $153 a day. That is a tax. It is a tax on the Canadian taxpayer and it is tax free to all those poor, poverty-stricken Senators over in the other place.
Look at them. If Senator Molson does not get that $153 a day, you know what will happen. The whole empire will dissolve. There will be no Hockey Night in Canada. It will be gone. Just think about it!
In fact, all they have to do is check in with the Clerk, walk in through the front door, walk to the back, and they get their allowance.
Brother Lawson was appointed by the Liberals and I assume that Liberals appoint only Liberals. Therefore he is really a Liberal. In fact these people sit over in the Senate, good Liberals and Tories, and all we have now is Allan MacEachen leading the Liberal forces in the Senate.
Of course, the Tories want to get the majority in the Senate. There is a rumour around that the Prime Minister is going to name 11 Senators and then he will have the majority so he can pass all these bills.
The Canadian people must ask in wonder, how can this lower House, the House elected by the people of Canada, countenance and stand and vote for what is being placed on their backs. I know how the member for Mississauga South is going to vote on this because those are his fat-cat friends and he is going to support them right to the hilt. He knows his day is coming, but it had better come before 1993.1 think there is a good possibility that the member for Mississauga South will end up in the Senate. I think you would make a fine senator-
High Commissioner to Uganda.
If ever there was a reason for putting a stop to the Senate right now, it is the thought that the hon. member for Mississauga South would end up in the Senate.
What about support?

He wants my support, Madam Speaker. Who am I? I am a member of Parliament opposed to the Senate. Why would I support you? We have denied Canadian people the opportunity for a guaranteed annual income, and these people sitting over in the other place have a guaranteed annual income to 75 years of age. Those who were there before the 75 year deadline came in or those who were grandfathered, some of them can go on forever.
Some of them do.

We are saying to the Canadian people, we cannot give you a guaranteed annual income. But to some people who are friends of those in high places, you could get into the Senate and in fact, you can actually get a guaranteed annual income to age 60 and after the seventy-fifth year get a nice pension. You could get an beautiful pension because there is an allowance for the pension in the Estimates and we are going to pass that.
It does not end at age 75. It continues and that pension is fully indexed because they are over 75. Yet we have said to old age pensioners in this country, we can't fully index your pensions. Isn't that something? Now we have a partial indexation. We cannot fully index the GST tax credits, for God's sake, we cannot fully index that. But, by golly, we can give $153 incentive a day to go to work. To go to work! Imagine what any trade unionist would give. He would give his eye tooth for an incentive over and above his hourly wage-
Or a single parent.

Or a single parent. In this country we nickel and dime poor people to death. We have all sorts of forms to fill out to see if you qualify with your income. You have to qualify, but people like those in the Senate have carte blanche. In closing, I call on members of this House to vote for the motion that eliminates the $47 million from the Estimates which then would put an end effectively to the flicks and flacks and other kinds of characters in the other place.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great attention to the discourse of our colleague and the profound words he just shared with us but I wonder whether Brother Lawson in the other place was listening attentively.
I want to ask my colleague from Nickel Belt that when he says he wants to cancel the budget of the Senate, and therefore abolishing it, is this the same Senate that was asked by his colleague for Yorkton-Melville when he said on the steps of Parliament Hill, on May 7, that he wanted that Senate to abolish the GST? Is this the same Senate he is referring to or is this something else and am
Supply
I misunderstanding it? Second, the Premiers and the Prime Minister are meeting right now to reform the Senate, and hopefully they may have arrived at a successful conclusion. I think all Canadians wish that. They want to amend the Senate and if they arrive at this unanimous agreement of all premiers and the Prime Minister to change the Senate, but nevertheless to continue having a Senate, does that mean that he wants to remove all the funding for that body of Parliament which may have today already received the unanimous consent of all the Premiers and the Prime Minister? I wonder if that is the specific proposition that he is entertaining. Perhaps he could clarify that for us.

I thank my colleague for the questions. I will answer the second one, first. He is too good a politician not to recognize that what will come out from across the street, from everything I have heard so far, is not that they will agree to include that idea of a Senate within the Meech Lake Accord. They are saying that that is an idea that might be discussed at a later time. That is my impression. I do not have the facts but I do not think that is the way it is. I do not think any of that will happen now. Meech Lake is not going to be amended to include the kind of Senate which you have just described.
We cannot get caught in the same trap again with respect to whether we are going to have a second chamber and how it will operate. It seems to me that the lesson we have learned from Meech Lake is that we need to hear from the Canadian people.
First of all, do we want the second chamber, how is it going to operate and what powers is it going to have or should it have? How will the representation from across the country be in the Senate? Will it be by region, constituency or by proportional representation? I think the Canadian people have to be consulted on that question. We are not going to have the same process again where 10 premiers and a Prime Minister sit around in a room and decide the form of parliamentary democracy for the next 50 generations. We are not going to go through that again. That is number one.

June 6, 1990

What I am suggesting is that we are helping to resolve this problem, because if the Senate was killed and we had to start from scratch, that would be the best way to go. Everybody talks about a triple-E Senate, but if you are going to elect the Senate, then it has to have power. And where is it going to get the power? Obviously, you are going to have to take the power from the House of Commons to give to it. Then you are going to end up with a system where you have to have a check and a balance and voila, we have harmonized into the American congressional system.
I do not know where you come from, but I cannot imagine this in my own head space that we could go ahead and let these men sit in the building across the way and develop this concept of a Senate without the Canadian people having an input. Surely, we are not going to do that again. Surely, that is the lesson of Meech Lake.
The first question the hon. member asked about our asking the Senate to kill the GST. The reality is that we have a policy and our aim is to work, wherever we get the opportunity, to get the Senate eliminated. We are taking this opportunity today to try to get the government to vote with us to abolish the Senate, but the Senate is a reality, it is there and it is dominated by Liberals. The Liberal Party in this House has said it is opposed to the GST and it voted against it. The Senate Liberals are members of the caucus of the Liberal Party in the House and surely the Senate Liberals have got to be consistent with the Liberal Party. That is what we are challenging you to do. That is the challenge, but the greater issue is to get rid of the Senate and we are taking the opportunity today.
Would you prefer to get rid of the Senate or get rid of the GST?
Well, we are killing two birds with one stone.
All Canadians are birds.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all Canadians have heard that the NDP prefer getting rid of the Senate to getting rid of the GST.
I want to ask a supplementary question of our NDP colleague. Notwithstanding the Meech Lake Accord and the unanimity clause of the Meech Lake Accord, which means that the Senate cannot be abolished or changed without the consent of all provinces, the NDP position right now is to breach the accord, even before it is fully passed by everybody, and get rid of the Senate notwithstanding everything else. That is the twofold statement that we heard.
One, it is better to get rid of the Senate than to get rid of the GST is the new NDP proposition which we have just heard right now through presumably their official spokesman on such issues. Second, notwithstanding the unanimity required under the Meech Lake Accord to get rid of the Senate, the NDP wants to do it unilaterally.
I do not think that my colleagues and I would agree with either one of those propositions.

I will try to draw the picture for my friend.
The first opportunity that the Senate had to deal with the GST was second reading. Everybody knows that second reading is in principle. If I recall, the Liberals in this House on second reading spun out the debate. They absolutely fought the GST in this House with us, toe to toe, jowl to jowl, body to body. Together we fought the GST at second reading because in principle we believed it was a flawed tax. That is what they said, a flawed tax.
Now, lo and behold, the first opportunity the Senate had to deal with the GST was at second reading. What happened? It went in there at 11.30 in the morning and second reading was finished at 11.45 a.m. on the same day. There was not one debate on principle on the GST in the other place, which is the most disastrous tax ever in the history of this country.
I am repeating what the Liberals said in this House. They have sent a message to Canadians. They have said that secretly they agree with the principle of this tax and maybe all they are going to do is patch it up here and patch it up there. So they showed their hand that in fact they do support the GST; it is just a matter of some cosmetics to fix it up and fix it up there.
Second, without a doubt, one of the problems that we have discovered about changing the institutions of government in this country are constitutional ramifications. Surely, the people of Canada have a right to participate in the form of government that will be in place. Surely,

June 6, 1990

that is a principle. Surely, that is something that we have learned from the Meech Lake experience.
The form of the other House, if there is to be another House, has to be dependent on what Canadians think. It has to be modelled on what Canadians think. We cannot go back to having 10 people and a prime minister sit down in one place and decide the form of government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The time for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate with the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden.

Madam Speaker, I have listened with interest to this debate. As a 40-year member of the democratic socialist movement in this country, I was very pleased with the motion moved by my colleague for Kamloops, and the speech by my friend for Prince George-Bulkley Valley. He is a couple of years younger than me.
The abolishment of the Senate has been a matter of history since the second convention of the CCF in 1935, and we have never wavered from that position. Our party has been consistent in that position for close to 55 years. So let us set that matter to rest now.
Our caucus, our party, and our leader have called upon the Senate to exercise its constitutional authority to delay, stop, or amend legislation that comes from the House of Commons. That is the reality. There is nothing we in this caucus can do about that.
What we have said is that it is about time the Senate earned its keep. It has a golden opportunity to add to what was said in this place, and said by about three-quarters of the Canadian people, on the goods and services tax. Since there is nothing we in our party can do about the constitutional authority and rights of the Senate until the Constitution is changed, all we have done is called upon the Senate to get off their backsides and do what they are supposed to do.
My colleague, the hon. member for Nickel Belt mentioned the second thoughts. My problem is, when did they ever have a first thought on the GST at second reading? Goodness knows if they will ever come up with a second thought.
Supply
I suppose I was under some delusion that the government would like this amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops. I listened to the Prime Minister, the government House leader, several other cabinet ministers railing away over the last number of months about a Senate of appointed bodies usurping the rights of the supreme body, namely, the House of Commons, an elected body, by delaying, amending and otherwise compromising government legislation. Well now, isn't that sad?
However, I thought that the motion by my colleague from Kamloops would make the government most happy. If members want to put an end to what the other place is doing to government legislation, pass this motion of my colleague from Kamloops tonight and cut them off at the pass, and that includes their $153 a day on any days they might show up.
I know a lot of senators and I have regard for them personally. Some of them have spent many years in public life, in parties different from mine. I have never questioned their loyalty to the country. I have never questioned their motives. I have questioned their sanity lots of times and they do the same to me and that is fair ball.
But if there is any one principle in a parliamentary democracy, and this is why I worry about what was going on across the road yesterday and today, the whole principle of representation by population is so fundamental and basic to a parliamentary democracy that there should not be any question about it.
If one reads some Canadian history going back to the conferences in Charlottetown 1864 to 1866, and a few other places, it was agreed to have a second chamber. It may not be common knowledge, but its primary responsibilities were twofold: one, so-called sober second thought; two, the protection of property. That was built into the reasons for having an appointed second chamber. The problem has been that there is nobody in the other place protecting the property of Canada, in other words, protecting this country.
As I said at the outset, I stand for the abolition of the Senate. I think it is an anachronism, at best. I am not trying to demand that the policy of my party should be implemented yesterday. I recognize the reality. The Senate is there and if we cannot get it abolished, we will get it elected. However, if it is going to be elected, then somewhere in the scheme of things the principle of

June 6, 1990
Supply
representation by population has to come into play. Typically Canadian, we compromise here and there on the size of constituencies, the amount of population in each one right across the country. That takes into account and recognizes our geography and where our people are located and we provide a margin of above or below the average. If we cannot get the Senate abolished, then we have to arrive at that compromise.
In fact, many years ago my beloved former colleague, the then member for Winnipeg North Centre, turned pale and went into shock when a former colleague of mine went into his office and said that we need to have two NDPers accept an appointment to the Senate. He asked: "Why would you want to do that?" and we said: "There will have to be two NDPers in the Senate to move and second a motion to abolish the damned thing, otherwise it will never happen". So, I am tempted to volunteer and maybe my good friends the hon. member for Kamloops or the hon. member for Brant would be willing to join me so we could get something started in the Senate to abolish it.
I mentioned earlier that I have listened to government members in this government, and even members of the previous Liberal government, complain vociferously about the activities of the Senate. It is more particularly germane to today's debate. Repeatedly, the Prime Minister, the government House leader, other cabinet ministers and members on the back-benches of the government have complained about the abuse of parliamentary democracy by unelected members of the Senate. Cutting off their funding puts an end to that abuse, to put it purely and simply.
Unless there are a lot of hon. members on the government side or in the Liberal caucus who are preaching for a call and an appointment to the Senate, surely they can do no other. I maybe should exclude the members of the Liberal caucus, but certainly the members of the government caucus who are outnumbered in the other place at the moment, which they will correct some time in October or November, if worse comes to worst. It is perfectly legal and constitutional; they will have a majority and they will get their bills through.
What has that got to do with a parliamentary democracy? It is just a continuation of what has been going on since 1867. They are not there to represent the ordinary people of this country. They are there supposedly to supply second thoughts. They are something like some of the born again Christians that I have run into. They did not learn any better the second time around; their second thoughts, so much for that.
They are also there to protect property. I get phone calls from people who are losing their house or losing their farm because of what the banks are doing, or even what an agency of this Parliament, the Farm Credit Corporation, is doing to farmers in my province and all other parts of Canada. I have small businessmen phone or ask me to drop around and see them. Where is the Senate? It is there to protect them and have been since 1867.
I doubt if any of these words in this Chamber today are going to get across the road, Madam Speaker, but you never know. They might. I think the First Ministers better think again. This is my own personal opinion because it is not party policy. However, I have the right in my caucus to express my personal opinion on this issue and others. All three parties better think again about the whole principle of representation by population, and margins can be made below and above the average in every province or every region of Canada.
I have listened to all three political parties in several provinces over the last 40 years complaining about the gerrymandering and the unbalanced representation in provincial constituencies, for example, if one provincial riding had 7,000 population and the other one had 12,000 or 15,000. I have listened to all three political parties complain about that ad nauseam in province after province, always when they were in opposition.
We negate the principle of representation by population at the peril of a parliamentary democracy, unless we keep in place the paramountcy of the House of Commons. If that is not there, I do not care what kind of Senate reform is brought in we lose the power of the commoners, we lose the authority of the commoners and the government of the day, even if an unbalanced Senate were elected. We have hit very hard at the foundations
June 6, 1990

of a parliamentary democracy. If there is nothing else we have inherited from the British and the French, it is that.
I object to resorting to copying the United States congressional system. God knows they are good neighbours and good friends, but I think the flaws in their system are a heck of a lot worse than the ones in ours.
I for one do not want to adopt the kind of system where a province like mine has x number of senators and another province with four or five times the population has the same number. If they are elected, what does that do to the foundation of a parliamentary democracy?
I have more faith in the Canadian people. Whether they come from Ontario, Newfoundland, or Saskatchewan their basic instincts of decency, civility, getting along together and keeping this country united will always come through. The problem has not been with our own people, except when we fail to provide some leadership and statesmanship. That is where the problem has been too many times in my 22 years here and years before that in active participation in the political process.
If nothing else I hope, because the government could bring in another motion tomorrow and carry it, that it gives a signal to the other place to cut the mustard or it is shut down. It has a constitutional right presently to defeat a government bill, amend it, or delay it. That has always been there. That is the reality, but, by the gods of war, if it wants to survive for at least four, five or six years-I predict that is about the limit of its life-it better start earning its keep.
That is why the NDP demands that members of the Senate stop the GST. They do not have to worry about polls or their own political parties. They can do whatever they want. They talk a good fight. Now is their chance. If they want to do something just for once to present some evidence that justifies their existence, then they better do it now. I think we should cut them off at the pass, tonight. Whatever the First Ministers come up with across the street that they agree on and that will implement Meech Lake, God bless them. I know it will be a big improvement, if they agree, over what we presently have.
I think no harm is done to this House or to this country if we cut off the funding for that other place, because as a famous British parliamentarian said "for what you have
Supply
done for as long as you have been here, you can do no more. In the name of God, go".
Please, Madam Speaker, I ask this House to pass the motion of my hon. friend for Kamloops.

Madam Speaker, I sat here and listened to my highly respected and hon. colleague from Regina-Lumsden. I have also sat and listened to the comments and questions made by others in relation to earlier speeches. I could not help but think that if we could induce the public to listen to the debate that has gone on over the last hour, indeed the spirit and essence of the debate would be such that we would be leaving the public totally confused.
On the one hand we have a group arguing that it is essential to abolish the Senate tonight. On the other hand we have another group arguing that the Senate should be in a position to stop completely and totally the goods and services tax legislation before it.
We have the argument from those who are proponents of abolishing the Senate that for them to ask the Senate to abolish the goods and services tax is in effect supporting the existence of the Senate.
It is a totally confused message that the public and those who care to take the time to listen to this debate tonight are receiving.
There is another interesting aspect to this issue too: if we were to support the motion of the member for Kamloops, which would effectively pull out the funding from the Senate, this would, I suppose in a practical sense eliminate the Senate. Further, if you carry this logic to its next conclusion, this automatically means the passage of the goods and services tax because without the Senate or the other place for the House of Commons to send its business for the so-called sober second thought, the goods and services tax bill would be a fait accompli. We would have the matter before us.
We have one argument to cut the funds from the Senate because we do not need the Senate. On the other hand, we are asking the Senate, although we do not believe in it, to discontinue its apparent support up to this time. There has been some argument about whether or not there was support for the goods and services tax at the second reading stage. We have people saying to eliminate the budget for the Senate, which will bring the Senate down and cause senators to have no place to

June 6, 1990
Supply
come to work. This would mean the passage of all these bills that are deemed so controversial.
I am totally confused by what message it is that we are intended to have conveyed to us. There are likely some people who are taking parts of my sentence and saying that the hon. member is probably confused most of the time. For those who only pick that out of my comments, I would say to listen to the entire sentence.
I offer some sympathy to my colleague, the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden. While he has conveyed to us that he is given the opportunity to speak freely with an open mind on any subject that he wishes whether or not it addresses his party's policy, he is caught between the proverbial rock and a hard place.
Does he really mean-and I say this in all sincerity- that the Senate, should not have any funds, which will mean the automatic passage of the goods and services tax? Is that what they really want? Or, do they really want the Senate which they do not believe in to step in and annihilate the goods and services tax? By the way, it is a tax about which members of the opposition have spent much time and effort in passing along half-truths to the public so that they are, as is most of the public, totally confused and baffled and object to the imposition of what is perceived to be a new tax?
I present that proposition to the hon. member. Does he not find himself on a shaky fence? I do not mean that he has placed himself there but, by virtue of the motion the hon. member for Kamloops has placed before us this evening, does it not leave him with a bit of a contradiction in principles?

I thank my colleague and friend from Regina-Wascana. I did not want to repeat the argument that has been put up numerous times today and in the previous few weeks.
We have stuck to our guns on a policy that goes back 55 years on abolishing the Senate. All we are doing is facing up to what we have to face today and over the last 55 years. The Senate is there. The majority of people supported the present government and the previous one on maintaining the Senate, so we lost. I am not complaining about that. In spite of that, a large body of
opinion in the country says either do something about it or get rid of it. I hope the latter point will gain sway.
Given that reality-and I said it in my remarks and I say it to my hon. friend-for once will they earn their keep? They are there to provide second thoughts. Just for a change they should protect the property of homeowners and farmers from the GST. They should protect the businesses of small business people by the thousands all over this country. Why do they not protect that property for a change instead of the property of the corporate few? I am not interested in those kinds of bodies being in a first or even second chamber of this place. We do not need it. They have victimized the people of this country for decades and they continue to do so.
May I remind my hon. friend what is going on among financial institutions these days. The Senate is silent about the farmers, the little store keepers and the homeowners in my riding and his as well. But when it comes to the property of the wealthy or the Toronto Stock Exchange, the bondholders, oh my goodness, that is their idea if protection of property. The Senate has failed to understand the reason and purpose for its existence, if there ever was one.
I make no apologies for the position my party has taken since 1935 and the position we are taking today. They either put up or shut up or we get rid of them, one or the other.
