speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to speak in support of the motion before the House.

I welcome the opportunity today to address the impact of the Main Estimates on housing. There have been allegations that the federal government has lost interest in housing and is letting the disadvantaged find for themselves. Nothing could be further from the truth.

As the Minister of State for Housing I ask all members of this House to support the approval of the Main Estimates for 1990-91. With respect to the $1,884 billion included in these spending estimates with respect to housing, I must point out to the House that over 90 per cent of the total included in Vote 25 is associated with commitments made in prior years.
These moneys are required as a result of the contractual obligations entered into by this government and former governments. These are obligations to provincial housing agencies and their reimbursements for expenses

June 6, 1990
Supply
which are being incurred as a result of these continuing commitments.
Within the remaining 10 per cent or less, most of the expenditures relate to planned 1990 social housing commitments in accordance with agreements between the federal government and the provinces that have been in place since 1986.
Approval of Vote 25 is essential if we are going to honour the commitments that we have made in the context of our current federal-provincial agreements, and if we are to allow the many non-profit groups to develop and proceed with the needed housing for low-income Canadians.
Finally, in the housing support expenditures that we have planned, the Estimates include some $32.3 million against $33.9 million in fiscal year 1989-90.1 should point out that there has been no increase in this proportion of CMHC's expenditures for several years.
Although planned new activity has been cut by some 15 per cent, many people do not realize that the budget is actually continuing to grow. In fiscal year 1989-1990, it is estimated that the federal government contributed some $1.7 billion in social housing assistance. In fiscal year 1990-1991, our total budget will increase almost $91 million.
We will not be able to increase the supply of assisted housing as far as we had planned, but we are still going to provide almost $90 million for new social housing in
1990.
Since forming the government we have been very upfront about the belief that the deficit must be reduced. If Canada is to enjoy a strong and growing economy, one which will increase the opportunities for all Canadians, we must demonstrate our readiness to manage effectively-
In the housing area we have made great strides since 1984. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has exemplified the the kind of good management that we need throughout all of the government. For example, the Mortgage Insurance Fund had a deficit of some $786 million in 1984 when the government came into office. Today that has been turned around to a position where it is solvent for the first time in a decade.
CMHC has made some very significant reductions in manpower as well, with a decrease of over 1,000 staff years since 1984, while at the same time improving its performance in a wide range of other areas. As a result of the last expenditure review, CMHC will have reduced its administrative costs associated with government programs by $3.5 million by 1991. In area after area, we have demonstrated the ability to reduce spending, to use assets more efficiently and to provide increased help where it is most needed.

Before 1984, federal government policies provided programs designed for various income levels. Two out of three households receiving federal assistance could afford housing on the private market. In the private sector, a series of intermittent programs cost hundreds of millions of dollars in subsidies which were found to be both ineffective and inequitable and even caused some distortion on the market.

The two main principles of our housing program since 1986 have been to direct social housing assistance to those most in need and to support rather than interfere with the effective functioning of the private housing markets.
Over the four preceding years, some 80,000 assisted housing units were produced, but only about 40 per cent of those were directed to those in need, perhaps some
32,000	households. In the four years since 1986 we have assisted some 75,000 low-income households, that in comparison with only 32,000 low-income households in the previous four years that the former government was in office.
In 1984, there were less than 135,000 housing starts in Canada. Since then we have averaged over 200,000 housing starts in this country each year. Preliminary numbers for May show that housing starts have actually not fallen this year but have stabilized somewhere around the 200,000 mark, and that in spite of the slowing down of the economic situation that we have seen in recent weeks. We could expect that there will be some drop-off in the number of housing starts, obviously in reaction to current interest rates, but this has not yet materialized and we are still in the neighbourhood of some 200,000 a year.
June 6, 1990

It is clear that we have provided more opportunities both in assisted housing and in the private market. But that certainly does not mean that the job is complete. In my travels across the country over the past year I have met with representatives of provincial, territorial and municipal governments, with members of the native community, members of the academic community, with people in every aspect of the housing industry and with people who are in real need.

I have listened to single parents who have trouble making a living; to native people in remote areas living in very difficult conditions; to higher income senior citizens and even to young couples who are working very hard to give their children a good start in life.

I have listened to the concerns these people have and to their ideas. I have seen the deplorable conditions that many face, even in a country as rich as ours.
Affordability is the most immediate concern, one which clearly cannot be resolved by the federal government acting alone. Canada is a vast country with very different regional environments in terms in both geography and history. The complexity of the situation is illustrated by the fact that a single municipal by-law could frustrate the efforts to provide affordable housing in any given area. I could have millions or billions more dollars in my budget and one single municipal by-law could destroy the effectiveness of that funding as far as affordable housing is concerned.
If all Canadians are to enjoy adequate and affordable housing, we require a concerted effort by all levels of government working together and working with the home building industry.
At the federal level we have been building on a strong foundation of our two guiding principles to address the shelter needs of low-income households within our social housing programs and, in the private market, for renters and aspiring homeowners.
Although there is still much to be done, we really have much to be grateful for here in Canada with respect to housing. We have a very mature home building industry which has met the challenge of housing for a growing population. In the short period of some 40 years, from 1941 to 1981, the number of dwellings in Canada was
Supply
increased from about 2.6 million to over 8.2 million. That is quite an achievement.
What is more, the percentage of homeowners has increased to the point that 62 per cent of households now own their own homes. That puts Canada ahead of most other developed countries in the world as far as giving its citizens an opportunity to acquire an equity hedge for their retirement years. This accomplishment is all the more dramatic when you consider that these mean a seven-fold growth in owner-occupied dwellings in our cities.
Over the five-year period since 1985, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has provided mortgage insurance on almost three-quarters of a million dwellings, allowing people to obtain a home of their own with a down payment as low as 10 per cent. This includes many first-time home buyers who were able to achieve the dream of homeownership only through the CMHC mortgage insurance program.
Canada has also developed a large supply of assisted housing providing shelters to some 637,000 households. This portfolio provides decent shelter and affordable rents in settings where the residents can enjoy security of tenure. Over the lifetime of each of these 637,000 dwellings, they will provide a home to many households in time of need. This portfolio is a major component of Canada's social safety-net. It represents a federal commitment this year alone of $1.8 billion in annual subsidies.
Our emphasis now is on preserving this societal asset and in utilizing it more effectively. Now we are looking for ways to serve more low-income households within our existing supply of assisted housing. In part, we are encouraging the project sponsors of projects committed under previous programs to fill vacancies with households in need.
I firmly believe that we need not only to provide decent shelter to low-income families and individuals, but to ensure that these people have the maximum opportunity to take hold of their housing needs, to shape their own communities, and to experience the pride of self and place which so many of us take for granted. Many of the residents of public housing have shown their readiness to play a greater role in the management of

June 6, 1990
Supply
their own projects and to contribute to the building of strong and safe communities.
The Doone Street project in Fredericton, New Brunswick, is just one example of what residents can do want they join forces. Not only did they create a drop-in unit headed by a local policeman, but they were able to get rid of community violence and intimidation in the project. At the same time, they were able to take on the exterior maintenance work for their own project, creating work for teenagers who to live in that project. They are also organizing spring clean-up programs in which the entire community joins with help from the project management.
That is just one example of many exciting ways in which tenants in public housing projects across the country have started to involve themselves in the actual management and running of those projects. We are doing our very best to encourage much more of that.
Recently, I wrote to my provincial colleagues, asking them for their co-operation in encouraging more of this kind of effort. I believe that the residents of public housing are ready, willing, and able to play meaningful roles in their own projects, homes, and environments.
I am pleased that most of the provincial response has been very positive to that. Already we have announced a set of initiatives to encourage increased resident participation in New Brunswick and I expect that we will be following that up very shortly with other similar announcements and similar efforts in all of the provinces where the provincial governments agreed to co-operate.
We have a lot to be proud of in our housing, but there are still areas of concern. Young families just starting out are finding that ownership is getting beyond their reach. The cost of homes is escalating much faster than they can afford to save.
Several factors are involved in this situation. One is that we are continuing to produce larger homes which attract second-time buyers but are unaffordable to those purchasing their first home. This is, in part, a reflection of the zoning in place in many areas of the country.
Another problem is that in some of the major centres, such as Toronto and Vancouver, there is a shortage of serviced land that is suitable for housing. We have built
up large areas of suburban sprawl that result in extensive travel to and from work, expensive and under-used service infrastructure, and often under-populated city cores.
[Translation}
The federal government has taken steps to deal with these problems. We have freed surplus government property in Toronto and Vancouver. In the Toronto area, for instance, this means developing new communities that will accommodate from 12,000 to 16,000 residents. Many of these new units will be affordable housing.
[English \
A few weeks ago I announced plans to redevelop some 16 properties in the Kitsilano area of Vancouver which are owned by CMHC. This initiative will ensure more appropriate housing to the existing tenants, many of whom are getting on in years, while it frees up land for other uses. It will be a hallmark of our commitment to both consultation and making better use of our land resources. I am sure that we are going to see many more residents utilizing that great federal asset than have in the past.
I have also announced our plans to redevelop the very land on which the CMHC Toronto branch is situated. That is another case of using what we have more effectively. Other sites are under active consideration at the present time.
Just last week I turned the first sod for the redevelopment of a major 43-acre site in the district of Burnaby, in British Columbia, where we will soon see the first new dwellings being built in what will become a new and integrated community of up to 1,200 people.
As I have said, the federal government cannot do all this alone. I am pleased to see that the mayors of Canada's major cities, in their caucus in the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, have recently joined in my call for a more concerted effort to address the housing affordability issue. This is why I have initiated the establishment of joint committees of all three levels of government to identify other potential lands and to overcome some of the roadblocks to meeting the needs for affordable housing. Such committees are already operating in a goodly number of urban centres across the country.
June 6, 1990

I mentioned the role of zoning and by-laws. Important as they are, we cannot allow them to be cast in stone so that they can prevent the realization of needed housing and the implementation of new approaches to better serve emerging needs. That is why earlier this year, I announced a program called ACT, Affordability and Choice Today. This is a co-operative program of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, the Canadian Home Builders, and the Canadian Housing and Renewal Association, funded by the federal government through CMHC.
The objective of ACT is to encourage reform of our system of by-laws to better reflect today's needs and to reduce the delays which can add so much to the cost of housing without adding any value.
We believe that consultation is the answer to many of our housing problems. We believe that with consultation we can benefit those who need housing. This is evident in our continuing work on developing housing options for seniors. Recently I have undertaken to have a series of housing conferences for seniors across the country. These are just some of the things that we have undertaken with respect to housing initiatives at the federal level over the last year.
The $1.8 billion in the Main Estimates for federal housing programs are absolutely essential if we are going to continue to meet the social housing commitments we have made over the years and if we are going to be able to produce even more social housing and help more Canadians to be housed better in this coming year. I urge the House to support the motion and vote to make sure we can assist the federal government to do a better job to house Canadians in the coming year.

Madam Speaker, I thank the minister for his remarks. I know he cares deeply about the very serious problem we have in the country today with affordable housing.
I want to ask him two questions. Right now young people cannot get the down payment required on many new large homes being built, especially in major markets. I would cite my own market, Toronto, as one prime example. Not only do they not have the money for the down payments, they also find when they do get a mortgage it is only for three or five years, and with the
Supply
fluctuation in interest rates there is no long-term stability. It is very frustrating for them and promotes a lot of insecurity in families.
Because this is a very trying and difficult time, would the minister consider asking Canada Mortgage and Housing to supply up to 100 per cent of the financing? At the same time, what is the longest period that Canada Mortgage and Housing is providing for mortgages with the current formula? It was not that long ago that you could have a mortgage for 15 and 25 years. I wonder why we could not get back to that.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the comments and remarks of the hon. member for Broadview- Greenwood. I know he too has a deep interest in making sure that Canadians have affordable housing, particularly in his and my city of Toronto. He specifically asked questions with respect to the amount of down payments or mortgage insurance which might be available and also the term of a mortgage.
I will start with his second question first and say there really is no limit on the term of a mortgage that Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will insure. If a buyer of a home wants to commit to a mortgage with a long term, they can very well commit to that and there is no problem providing insurance as was common a number of years ago.
Unfortunately, because of the interest rate situation and the fluctuations in interest rates over the last few years, many people gamble that they will fall and so accept shorter term mortgages, sometimes as short as six months. As the hon. member points out, sometimes three years or five years but not the longer term mortgages we used to see. It is not because it is not available, it is that the actual borrowers are interested in getting their interest rate as low as possible and then lock themselves into a longer term commitment.
In the last four years we have provided a new program called "mortgage backed securities". A mortgage backed security allows for an investor in securities to sell those securities and provide a secondary market for the securities, which were not available prior to four years ago when the mortgage backed security form was introduced by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the federal housing agency.

June 6, 1990
Supply
At the time, it was hoped that the MBS, the mortgage backed security, would allow investors to feel they could give longer term mortgages, because they could always be sold. There would be a secondary market for their mortgages, and they would feel protected.
The mortgage backed securities have been very successful and billions have been put on to the market. It is a very well accepted program. Unfortunately, in spite of all that, the actual borrowers, the home purchasers or home buyers by and large have been unwilling to commit to longer term mortgages. I suspect it is because they feel that, while interest rates may be "x" today they will be "x minus y" tomorrow. They want to get in and take advantage of the lower interest rates.
I am not sure that answers completely the hon. member's question with respect to the term of mortgages, but I will be announcing shortly some further details with respect to a housing financing conference this fall. We will be looking at all aspects of housing financing, particularly for first time home buyers. We will be examining all the various options that anybody has ever thought of that might be available, to see if there is not a way we can improve the situation with respect to the financing aspect.
The hon. member also asked a question about 100 per cent insured mortgages. As he is aware, now one can obtain an insured mortgage with a down payment of up to 10 per cent. We are exploring this very carefully, and hopefully before too long we will have a 95 per cent insured mortgage with a 5 per cent down payment in place. Quite frankly, there are many people who feel concerned with down payments that are as low as 5 per cent. I guess it is against that concern that one has to balance off the thought of having a 100 per cent insured mortgage and a zero down payment.
Those things have been tried in the past. However, I think it is important that there be some personal commitment by the people buying a home so that they know they have their own stake in the home and it is not just the stake of the taxpayers involved. Still, we are pursuing very vigorously the concept of a 5 per cent down payment and 95 per cent insured mortgage. We are going to be holding this conference on financing housing this fall, which I am sure the hon. member will find very interesting.

Madam Speaker, I thank the minister for a very able presentation of his motion.
The presentation of his motion is more able than the government's performance. I am sure he will be able to comment on figures that were presented to us by the Canadian Home Builders' Association concerning what it thinks is the main cause for the disastrous decline in housing starts, which it finds in the interest rate rise.
The Canadian Home Builders' Association commented that first time home buyers who could afford 10 per cent mortgage rates number about 96,000. It requires an income of $51,500, and that includes 24 per cent of all buyers. When the mortgage rates went up to 14 per cent and the income required was $67,500, instead of 96,000, there were less than half. There were 40,500 who could afford it. This is 10 per cent of all potential buyers.
I am wondering what the hon. minister can tell us about the government's plans to relieve the situation of home buyers, home builders, construction workers, furniture makers, material suppliers and all the other many thousands who depend on the building of homes, either to use them or to produce them. If a rise in mortgage rates from 10 per cent to 14 per cent cuts the number of possible buyers to less than half, can the minister assure us, either that the interest rates will soon come down and enable people to buy homes again or that the schemes he has been telling us about will, in spite of the high interest rates, be able to bring the percentage who can afford to buy a home up from 10 per cent to 24 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister. There is very little time left.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina for his question. As the hon. member is aware, there are a number of factors involved in the question of affordability of housing. One factor is the amount of the monthly payment and that is impacted by interest rates. Other factors relate to the price of the house itself.
Recently, many people have been saying that Canadians should really be applauding the fact that housing prices are now starting to fall and indicating that perhaps it was necessary that we have a situation like that if we are going to avoid a real disaster in the future, so that we can make sure that for future generations housing will be
June 6, 1990

affordable. When housing prices go up, they cause problems. When housing prices come down, they cause problems. All of this, unfortunately, does not help the situation for people who want to buy houses.
At the same time, I would like to assure the hon. member that many of the programs that we have now under way, including the development of surplus federal government lands for first time home buyer housing in the metropolitan Toronto and the Vancouver areas, other initiatives that we hope we will have on stream before too long such as the 5 per cent down payment, all will help the affordability situation and will certainly help people to be able to buy homes, people who cannot buy them now.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise and talk about a very important matter, the question of affordable housing. In the Estimates the government is seeking approval of some $1.8 billion. I do not believe this truly represents the situation in Canada today with respect to those people who are seeking affordable housing, be it the home owner, the people in rental accommodation, people wanting to renovate their homes, the single parent, people of social assistance, seniors, or the physically challenged, who are finding it more and more difficult in respect of housing affordability.
While I applaud the efforts of my friend, the Minister of State for Housing, it is the government's lack of a sense of urgency and lack of commitment to housing which troubles me and troubles Canadians generally. I want to say that the stark reality of what is happening in this country cannot be disregarded any longer. While the minister paints a picture that would suggest, "Don't worry, be happy, although we are going through some difficult times, the situation is not as bad as it looks".
Let me deal first with the question of home ownership and what it means to those people who want to keep that dream of owning a home. My colleague spoke of the situation in Toronto and other centres. CMHC has projected that the industry will continue to build something like 200,000 homes this year. In fact, not only has the minister said that, but the former minister and the Minister of State for Privatization have spoken about the fact that the situation is stabilizing, that there is no need
Supply
to get too excited about the fact that there seems to be a slowdown in the construction industry.
The Toronto home builders and the Canadian home builders have tried to tell the government that 14.5 per cent interest rates are killing their industry. It is not only killing the dreams of people but killing the industry. Not
200,000	homes will be built in 1990-91 but only somewhere between 160,000 to 170,000 homes will be built in the next year. What that means is you have a lot of people who cannot buy these homes because they have become unaffordable as a result of high interest rates. Second, the construction industry and other related industries from window manufacturers to durable goods manufacturers are all starting to lay off people.
The industry is trying to tell the government, CMHC and the finance minister that 25 per cent to 30 per cent are already being laid off. The minister would want you to believe that don't worry, be happy, 200,000 homes will be built next year, the fact is that people cannot afford to buy the homes and the industry is declining very quickly. I hope that CMHC and the minister will meet with these people at the earliest possible opportunity to get the facts right because housing is not only good economics, it is good social policy.
I want to cover a number of topics, especially as they relate to the $1.8 billion that this government commits to people and social housing. I can tell you that if you look at the stark statistics of what is happening in this country, you will see that there are over 1.3 million households in the country that are paying more than 30 per cent of their income toward housing. There are close to 600,000 Canadians across this country paying over 50 per cent of their income toward housing.
Mr. Speaker, I do not have to tell you that is not only a serious economic problem for Canadians but a serious social problem as well. If Canadians cannot afford to pay their rent, or have to pay more rent, they will have to deprive themselves of certain things such as clothing and food. That is why you have over 500,000 people going to food banks each and every day, because it is too expensive for them to live.
I want to deal with this government's commitment to social housing. While the minister has paraded around the country saying: "Give my government hell so that I can do my job and get some more money to help people and so that the non-profit groups and the co-operative

June 6, 1990
Supply
groups get more money so they can build more units", every time he comes out of the cabinet room, he comes out with less for housing.
In this year alone there was 15 per cent less for social housing. In the next five years there will be $165 million less for social housing. Over the past four or five years, the government promised the co-operative sector to build 5,000 units to help the thousands of people on waiting lists from B.C. to Newfoundland to Ontario. Every province has waiting lists and people looking for affordable housing.
The co-operative sector was a way of being able to achieve affordability. In 1986 the government promised
5,000	units a year. We are at the end of the five-year term and in not one year did the government provide enough funds to build those 5,000 units. This year it will only be able to fund 1,500 units. Last year it funded 2,000. The year before it may have funded 2,500. What happened to the commitment to the 5,000 units each and every year for co-op housing and for the people who want to share in collective ownership? The government's commitment has been worth absolutely nothing. The whole program is threatened with cancellation because the minister and CMHC is reviewing the co-operative program.
I attended the meeting of the Co-Operative Housing Federation in Edmonton on the weekend. They are seriously concerned that this government will kill co-op housing and kill the opportunity for thousands of people across the country to have affordable housing.
Mr. Speaker, it is also very clear that in this country the homeless and people seeking affordable housing want a government that is responsive to their needs. As I have said, over the past four or five years, we have had a government that talks a good line but in actual fact has shifted the responsibility of housing more and more in each and every year to the provinces and the municipalities. In fact, the minister says tonight that governments cannot interfere in the private market-place. However, they are interfering in the market-place, especially when they will not do anything to lower interest rates.
When the Minister of Finance and other ministers say that it is essential to keep high interest rates to deal with inflation, the fact remains that people paying 14.5 per cent interest rates are potentially going to lose their homes. I think it is important for this government to realize that it can be a full partner in the housing issue. It should realize that it has the provinces, the municipalities, the non-profit sector, the co-operate and private sector which are all working together, and can essentially deliver affordable housing if there is a willing partner in the federal government.
The federal government cannot continue to say to Canadians that it is not its responsibility, that is the responsibility of the provincial government to do something. It has a prime responsibility, as it has in the past. CMHC is the federal agency that produced many homes after the war and worked with provinces and municipalities to achieve the housing objectives that we have for this country. Yet, slowly but surely since 1984, this government has taken itself out of the true partnership that must exist to deal with the housing problems.
We believe that if you house people and give them the opportunity for affordable housing, you will not increase the deficit, you will not have to increase government expenditures but in actual fact, you may decrease them. We know for a fact that subjecting people to inadequate housing or the problems of high-cost housing causes social and family problems. It causes crime and drug problems. In turn, that will cost not only the federal but provincial and municipal governments millions of dollars in extra expenditures. Providing a decent home for every Canadian in this country is the best way to deal with not only shelter, but social problems. We believe the two have to work in tandem.
We as a party some year and a half ago travelled across the country and talked with homebuilders, co-operative people, the non-profit sector, tenants, municipalities, and provincial governments. Across the country we went and essentially the message was clear. Everyone was saying that the federal government must become more involved, must exercise its leadership in housing, be prepared to bring in those programs and be prepared to work with the other levels of government and the other sectors to bring affordability back to housing. We have not seen that.

Our party laid out in our task force report some 25 recommendations that deal with how we believe the housing problems can be solved in this country. They talk about forging those new partnerships which are important and looking at ways of changing those financial instruments with generation mortgages, long-term mortgages, lower interest rates and getting rid of the GST that is going to add at least 2 to 2.5 per cent on the cost of a house, even after the rebates. There are a number of things that can be done to bring affordability back into the equation. We would like the commitment of this government to continue co-op programs with at least
5,000	units per year. We want more social housing built in combination with perhaps the private and non-profit sector working together. We also believe there needs to be recognition for the working poor and people on social assistance. Perhaps their income is not adequate to cover the expenses of their home. There needs to be some consultation and co-ordination with the provincial governments for topping up provisions of income, especially when you have the supply side problem and you are not able to build enough units. There is an opportunity to help those people who are paying more than 30 per cent, or more than 50 per cent of their income, on shelter.
There is another opportunity to deal with the private sector more effectively. The Canadian Homebuilders' Association and other homebuilders across the country should be freed from some of the red tape that exists at the municipal, provincial and federal levels of governments so that they can in fact start to produce the homes that people want and can afford to buy.
We also have to recognize that not everybody wants to buy a home. They have to live in rental accommodation. We know what interest rates are going to do to the supply side and to rental accommodations. Builders will not build. Investors will not invest in buildings when they know that interest rates are 14.5 per cent and climbing. Fewer rental buildings and apartments will be built, exacerbating the problem and the existing waiting lists.
We also believe that this government has shown callous disregard in the renovation market for the existing rental stock. We used to have a fantastic program, RRAP, but it has now been cut by this government.

That was one way of being able to rehabilitate our existing stock so that people could have affordable housing. Again this government has cut the housing budget. At the same time it wants us to believe that it is sincere and sensitive to the plight of the people in this country and yet it cut these worth-while programs which in fact provided affordable housing.
Our report and our consultation with Canadians has indicated that we need the reinstitution of the RRAP. We believe there is an opportunity for existing stock to be rehabilitated.
We believe that financial institutions have a very big part to play in delivering affordable housing, possibly the development of innovative mortgage instruments. We also believe there is an opportunity for the government to look at community land trusts so that within a co-operative or a non-profit area equity participation or capitalization could be added so that those groups can in fact generate internal capital for other projects.
There are a number of great opportunities in housing but we believe that this government needs to be committed. I do not question the commitment of this minister whose background in municipal government is well known. But I do question the commitment of his government which, over the past four or five years, has slashed budgets, removing responsibility from the federal government and trying to pass it off to the provincial and perhaps the municipal governments.
Finally, I want to speak again of something important. It is not only a question of money and housing.

The minister recognizes full well that if we can use the talents of and involve the private sector, the non-profit sector, the municipalities, and the provincial governments working together to solve the housing problems- and I agree it is complex and not simple-we can get back to the principle of housing affordability. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate all the comments of the hon. member for London East. I felt, however, that we should make sure that the record is straight with respect to the co-op housing situation.
The hon. member well knows, as do I, that five years ago the government and the co-op housing movement entered into discussions aimed at arriving at a program which would produce, both sides hoped, some 5,000 units of co-op housing a year. That arrangement was based on certain assumptions with respect to the mortgage vehicle being used, the ILM mortgage vehicle, and assumptions with respect to the real interest rate that could be achieved. The real interest rate anticipated by the Co-op Housing Federation of Canada was some 4 per cent.
The amount of money that was put into that program by the government at the time was an amount which both sides agreed could produce 5,000 units of co-op housing
a year, with a real interest rate on an ILM mortgage of 4 per cent. Unfortunately, as the executive members of the co-op housing movement quite readily agree, we have been unable to achieve that real interest rate of 4 per cent on ILM mortgages. That is the reason we have been unable to reach the target that was agreed upon of
5,000	co-op housing units each and every year.
If we can get the real interest rate on a co-op mortgage down by just 1 per cent, we can increase by 20 per cent the number of co-op housing units that the same number of subsidy dollars will provide.
One of the problems with co-op housing with respect to the government's policies, the policy of targeting all of its funds to the core needy people, is that by definition co-op housing is not core needy people exclusively but is also a range of people so as not to ghettoize poor people all in one place. It does have a range of incomes, which means people with a range of incomes are benefiting from some form of government subsidization.
The program is up for review this year, it being the fifth year of the commitment, as the hon. member knows. Are the hon. member and his party fully committed and supportive of continuing a co-op housing program in this country?

Mr. Speaker, of course our party is fully supportive of the co-op program. I would like to remind the minister that it was the Liberal Party which, some 22 years ago, introduced the whole concept of co-operative housing in this country.
I must remind government members that between 1980 and 1984, 30,000 co-operative units were built in this country-6,000 units a year for five years. We lived up to our commitment to the co-operative housing movement of some 30,000 units.
I can assure the minister that he will not have any difficulties from this side of the House when the budget comes down next year, hopefully, and co-op housing is very much a part of it. If he wants to commit 5,000 units on behalf of the government to the co-operative housing movement, he will not get any complaints from this side of the House. I am sure he will not get any complaints from the NDP either.
I should point out to him that I am happy to see that he is committed to co-op housing and that he is looking at ways to improve the ILM instrument so that in fact it can be the mechanism by which to provide those housing

units. However, if in fact it cannot be because of high interest rates, and if the real interest rates cannot be 4 per cent once inflation is taken into account, I hope that this minister will look at other ways of being able to come up with the money so that 5,000 co-op units can be built in the next five years.

Mr. Speaker, I note that the motion would remove $1,883 billion and some odd from the Estimates for housing. Surely the member wants to withdraw his motion.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House tonight to address a subject that concerns many Canadians who are waiting for government assistance.
I am referring to individuals, families and senior citizens who are looking for affordable housing, people who depend on government to provide them what many of us consider normal; people who, like us, want to live decently, with dignity; people who, without our assistance, will have to make incredible sacrifices to give their children a roof over their heads; people who without assistance may not even be able to make these sacrifices and thus will not have a home.
Every day, members rise in Parliament to announce that a given industry, province or city needs help. Every day, the government explains how it establishes priorities and what its strategy is. In many ways, the situation of a single mother who is looking for decent housing for her children is similar to that of someone who has lost her home or job.
There are also many analogies between senior citizens coping with rent increases and workers who earn little and are hard pressed to make both ends meet. These people have in common a need for a government that cares.
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I are concerned about what will happen to these people. We feel the need to give them a hand, and we do that, but not as often as we would like.
That makes us mad. Mad because in spite of all the resources this great country has to help the needy, the government-the government of all Canadian-must cut down its expenditures as a result of the ill-conceived programs and unpaid bills which the previous administration left behind when it was turfed out.
The government is prepared to lend a hand, but it has difficult decisions to make about the numerous demands

June 6, 1990
Supply
made on the public treasury. That is responsible government. Elad this kind of leadership prevailed earlier we would not find ourselves in the financial mess left after two decades of unsound budget management.
As I followed the proceedings of the Charest Commission I was deeply touched by the remarks of a witness who recalled his childhood as a Metis living in Saskatchewan, in a shed. Ele struck our heartfelt emotions as Canadians. Mr. Speaker, what that man had to say means more to me than all the learned arguments about the constitutional basis of federal spending powers. As I listened to him I came to understand that these powers were rooted not only in the law of the land but also in its heart. In its heart because as he was speaking I was saying to myself that never again should he and his children have to bear the cross of poverty and that Canada should continue to offer housing programs which give the less fortunate among us the opportunity to live in dignity and to become productive citizens.
Mr. Speaker, the measures which this government has been taking since my colleague, now Minister of National Defence, addressed this Elouse at the end of 1985 are aimed at those most in need of government assistance. The aim of the measures taken by the government when it revised its housing policy remains unchanged. The government is determined to pool the resources of all levels of government and community groups so they can be used to help the needy.
We are trying to find ways to respond more quickly to the needs of poor families and do a better job than the Liberal government that preceded us. And we are doing just that. During the past four years, since we announced our new policies we have managed to help 75,000 low-income households, while the Liberal government assisted only about 32,000 during the last four years of its term. Mr. Speaker, that is an improvement. It means
43,000	households more than the Liberal, over the same period of time. It means 43,000 households, families, single mothers, people on modest incomes, native people living on or off the reserve, handicapped Canadians and senior citizens.
Perhaps some of my colleagues, those who challenged this government's performance in the housing sector, are already aware of these developments but would rather not talk about them.
Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not intend to ignore the government's performance in the housing sector. In fact, the important thing is not necessarily what the government has done but the fact that it did so at a time when so many other major issues tended to focus public concern.
There is a lot to be said about this government's achievements in the housing sector. As a start, I would like to mention a situation that tells us a lot about this government's leadership. I am thinking of families living in large urban centres like Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, Vancouver and Winnipeg, as well as those living in smaller centres or rural regions; I am thinking of families with children, single-parent families, families on welfare and low-income families.
Mr. Speaker, these families now have increased access to subsidized housing. The present government, whose performance in the housing sector is being challenged, has used its influence to get provinces, municipalities and community groups to agree to focus more attention on the needs of the disadvantaged.
This government, which is being accused of lack of leadership, has managed to convince all parties concerned about easing the burdens of those who are in need to join forces and give these people access to more affordable and safe housing of the right size and quality. You won't read about this in the papers, but it's a fact. That is one example of the kind of leadership we provide.
Another example, Mr. Speaker, is native people. In many ways, they deserve our greatest attention. I was referring to them when I said that families should no longer have to live in poverty. As never before, these people have the attention of this government and its action in the field of social housing. Nearly half the housing provided in rural areas under the housing program for rural and native people is now used to meet the urgent needs of natives who live outside the reserves. That is an example of our commitment. Think of how successful the program for native people in urban areas is and of the money for natives living on reserves.
Mr. Speaker, I think hon. members do not want to hear about our successes. Neither do they want to hear that our government has shown enlightened leadership, a sign of effective and responsible management.
June 6, 1990

This commitment to work with native people, to offer them the best programs to meet their special needs, continues while the government holds wide-ranging consultations with native communities.
In the speech he gave to the House this evening, the Minister of State for Housing reiterated his commitment and this government's commitment to better housing for Canadians. The initiatives he has taken in the past and the energy he devotes to the housing portfolio clearly show his deep conviction that the government will find a solution to Canadians' housing problems.
But the minister does not boast about his achievements. In my opinion, that is the very essence of leadership. A leader does not spend his time recalling his successes and his accomplishments but he looks to the future, considers new challenges and shows the way.
There is no lack of challenges. In fact, the Minister of State for Housing has met them head on. Some examples are the exhaustive search for suitable housing for senior citizens; joint committees of all three levels of government set up by the minister across Canada, in order to take a collective approach to improving housing affordability; the new ACT program based on eliminating barriers and reducing delay in this area; the minister's efforts to release surplus federal land for housing purposes; his commitment to involving tenants in the management of subsidized housing; and his efforts to promote the tertiary sector. If we look at the facts, we have to admit that the poor have never been better served, and I really have trouble with claims that the government has failed to show leadership in the housing sector. I say that the people who make these claims have no idea of the meaning of the word leadership, and that they either do not know the facts, or, for obvious political reasons, prefer to ignore them.
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my speech this evening, I pointed out that our government was committed to helping the needy but also had to balance its concerns because of the urgent need to control government spending and put the government back on a sound financial basis. I can already hear members accusing us

of every possible evil; of being guilty of fighting the deficit at the expense of the poor. Nothing could be further from the truth.
Consider the amount we expect to spend on subsidized housing during the current fiscal year: nearly $1.8 billion, or $90 million more than last year. If an increase of this magnitude means reducing the deficit at the expense of the poor, perhaps my colleagues owe the House an explanation of their concept of mathematics.
But they might say that their real concern is that spending is not rising as fast as it should, but then how fast should it rise?
Mr. Speaker, that is not how to run a government. A responsible government balances its needs, takes into account its financial obligations and creates wealth that will make it possible to continue and, who knows, to improve the programs we will require.
We hear that the 15 per cent reduction in spending growth announced by the finance minister in his latest budget is not justified. But when will we hear them explain that in spite of this reduction, our government's ability to reach more needy families and seniors will continue to exceed the levels reached under the policies supported by the Official Opposition? Mr. Speaker, our government's housing record is beyond reproach and we have in front of us tangible proof that everything is being done to make the best use of the available financial resources.
Our country maintains noble and exciting principles but has come to recognize that to pursue these lofty goals effectively, it must have a sound economic foundation and forever vigorously ensure that it obtains good value from its programs.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before us is a motion to delete $1,883,690,000 from the budget of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Obviously, it was a tongue-in-cheek motion put forward by the member for London East and his colleagues since they do not seriously expect that it would be possible for this government-nor would they want it-to default on its mortgage payments which constitute 90 per cent of that amount. Thus it will be necessary to vote in favour of the motion so as not to worry the banker friends of the Liberal and Tory Parties.
It is really difficult to defend the government's program. The fact is that under this government the housing program has declined, and the previous minister responsible for housing was quite explicit about it. When he called for consultation, he did not say about what, he just said: "Give me your views". People told what kind of housing they thought was needed and then he said, "Well, there is going to be less" and he started reducing the social housing program in particular.
At that time, the home builders' association said, "That's fine, just leave us alone. We don't want subsidy for profit housing." Of course, the government was glad to take it at its word. Now we are having the further word from the home builders' association, which I will touch on in a few minutes.
The fact is that this government has been, year by year, retreating from providing housing to people for whom the market does not provide. There simply is going to be no program at all very soon. The government has excused these retreats as being necessary in order to help the core need housing, housing for those who fit their criteria as being needy. However, the core need programs, this year, were cut by 15 per cent and there is
June 6, 1990

good reason to fear that there will be more cuts in the years to come.
The government also cut the rental RRAP program, the program for rehabilitating old housing that low-income people can afford. On the whole, this government has shown that it wants to hand over the responsibility for housing to the provincial and municipal levels of government and get out of it itself.
That is interesting because its alleged reason for doing that is a shortage of money. Even the minister admitted that he would have liked to have more social housing, but he suggested there was not enough money for it.
There is, of course, enough money to increase the military budget by well over $500 million dollars. There is enough money to increase the budget for the secret police, CSIS, by $33 million. When it is for guns for white men, there is money. When it is for housing, especially for lower-income women and children, all of a sudden we seem to be running out of money.
Even as it stands, there is still left, perhaps, $180 million to assist with needed housing. With the money that it is giving to the military budget instead, including the arms manufacturers, the high-profit industry, the government could have increased that by two or three times easily, but that is not the government's budget priority. In fact, the record of the government has been watched, through these years, by the Canadian Housing and Renewal Association. On February 21 it stated, and I quote:
Despite the budget papers assurance that funding for social housing has grown substantially over the last five years, average expenditures in social housing as a percentage of total federal housing expenditures actually fell by almost 20 per cent in the second half of the decade compared to the 1980-84 period.
The minister has referred to the problem of high real interest rates. If he really feels that is a problem, I wish he would consult with his colleague, the Minister of Finance. We have been telling him all year to bring interest rates down. The comedy is that he gives the same answer as his predecessors gave. When I came to the House, in 1981, my first question was whether the government would bring the interest rates down. We were told the government was keeping the interest rates up in order to fight inflation. Nine years later, we get the same nonsense. Keeping the interest rates up in order to
Supply
fight inflation is like burning a house down in order to make room for housing. It just does not get you any housing.
The fact is that as the Canadian Housing and Renewal Association has said:
Now we are faced with increased pressure on provinces and
municipalities to come up with social housing assistance funds.
This is only one aspect of many programs on which the federal government is passing on its social responsibilities to the governments that have the lower ability to tax. This government prefers to fund the more high profit enterprises such as arms manufacture.
I mentioned that the Canadian Home Builders' Association has given us some figures on this matter in their brief entitled "A Crisis of Confidence". It is about the housing industry crisis. It points out that in Toronto, new home sales are collapsing. There are only 85,000 sales expected in 1990, which is down 80 per cent from the 40,869 sales recorded in the peak year of the current cycle, 1986. In fact, it is 63 per cent below the average annual sales during the entire decade of the 1990s.
There are people who do not live in Toronto who think everything is all right there. They should come and look at the people who are literally sleeping on the streets, in stairwells, in transit shelters, or in subways. Those are some of the people who have not left town.
A couple of years ago, the employees of Toronto Hydro went on strike and gave one fine reason for it. They wanted to be able to live in the town that they helped to build and maintain. They wanted to be paid enough for providing electric services to live in the city to which they provide the services. They were tired of commuting, perhaps an hour or two hours each way, in order to live in a cheaper place outside the city and come into it to work. The city would not allow them to live there because it would not pay them enough for housing.
The housing problem in Toronto is quite severe. The problem is not only in Toronto, of course, but it is most severe in Toronto of all Canada.
The majority of people in Toronto do not live in dwellings they own. The majority of people are tenants, so we could look at the rental field. CMHC did a survey and, in 14 out of 27 markets, it found that the vacancy rate is less than 3 per cent. That is getting pretty tight.

June 6, 1990
Supply
The government is doing nothing to help with rental housing.
I want to emphasize the point, because 3 per cent may sound very good in some places. In Toronto, the vacancy rate is 0.7 per cent; in Hamilton, 0.9 per cent; in St. Catharines, 1.9 per cent; in Kitchener, 1.3 per cent; and in Sudbury, not exactly a metropolis, but a hardworking town of miners and other producers of natural resources, people are having difficulty providing or finding housing. Sudbury has the lowest vacancy rate, 0.6 per cent. In Oshawa, it is 1.6 per cent. In Oshawa, a General Motors town, people cannot find enough housing to provide rental at a reasonable rate of turnover and a reasonable vacancy rate.
In Ottawa-Hull, the vacancy rate is 2.3 per cent; in Vancouver, 0.9 per cent; and in Victoria, 0.7 per cent. There simply is not enough rental housing available, not only in Ontario and not only in Toronto.
The problem is not only a shortage of decent housing for people to live in, it is also a shortage of employment.
The homebuilders' association pointed out that, at the peak of the recent housing cycle, 1987, there were
165,000	person-years of employment generated by housing in the Toronto area. But for 1990, it is barely half of that, with 88,000 fewer person-years of employment. In fact, that is a little less than half.
For this year, it is expecting less than half the jobs that there were three years ago directly and indirectly generated by housing. It would be the lowest year since the recession year of 1982. On the 1990 projected sales of only 8,500 units, it expects a good deal fewer jobs in 1991. One cannot get much tax revenue from people-whether it is income tax or the goods and services tax loaded more heavily on the low income-if they do not have income. When those housing jobs drop off, it is going to be felt in the revenues.
The homebuilders' association is quite explicit about what it thinks is the principle cause of this downturn. It is the interest rate policy of the government which is hurting the building industry. The association has been warning about it and their brief now gives fairly sharp figures.
It can be argued that there are other costs as well. Of course, land costs are something that both this government and the Ontario government are willing to allow to grow out of reason. They are not willing to impose a tax on speculation which was done for three years in the mid-seventies by the Ontario government and it was quite successful in cooling down land prices. Generally speaking, it is the cost of building a house that is becoming prohibitive.
The homebuilders' association points out in a chart that, when interest rates are at 8 per cent, 34 per cent of people can buy houses. When they jump to 10 per cent, only 24 per cent of the people can buy houses. At 12 per cent mortgage rates, only 16 per cent of people can buy houses. At 14 per cent-and we have gone beyond that now-only 10 per cent of the people can buy houses. When they go up to 16 per cent-and there is no reason to assure us that they will not go up-only 7 per cent will be able to buy houses.
The homebuilders have pointed out that this 14 per cent mortgage rate more than halves the number of potential first-time buyers able to afford a $150,000 home in the Toronto area. Mr. Speaker, I can tell you there are not very many $150,000 homes in the Toronto area. That is a relatively cheap home in Toronto. Therefore, it is the government's policy of high interest rates which is the chief factor in reducing the supply of housing and the supply of housing employment.
The homebuilders' association points it out in a different way. It has a chart that is too small to display and, of course, displaying it would be contrary to the rules of the House. I will point out that in 1981 and 1982, when the interest rates were high, the new home sales were low. Then through 1983-84-85, the interest rates came down and new home sales went up. In 1986-87-88, the new home sales were fairly high while the interest rates stayed low, except for one dip in the middle of 1987.
Since 1988, the interest rates have been climbing and the new home sales are declining. Interest rates are up and home sales are down. That is the pattern shown very clearly on this chart. The future is not very bright either in this matter. Gordon Thompson, the President of the CHBA, the Canadian Home Builders' Association, has predicted:
- that what happened in Canada in the early 1980s could happen again.

June 6, 1990

He is referring, of course, to the recession which he maintains was caused partly by the high interest rates on housing, and I remember that. There happened to be a by-election in Spadina in 1981 and I was hearing daily about people who were forced out of their homes. When the interest rate jumps and a working person goes to renew the mortgage on a home and finds that the payments have jumped by one-third or one-half over what they were before, but his or her salary or wage has not jumped by one-third or one-half, it means that he or she loses, not only the home but all the money that was put into it.
Mr. Thompson goes on:
The decline in housing sales led to layoffs, many firms left the industry, and land development slowed to match the level of demand. When demand recovered in the second half of the 1980s, shortages of labor, materials and land all combined to produce a serious escalation in housing prices.

recession, the very thing this government claims it is trying to avoid.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my colleague from Trinity- Spadina who I regard as being very sincere and conscientious.

The situation was this. My wife and I had put our life savings together and bought a 12-suite apartment block. In that era, it was generally conceived that if one had a 25 per cent down payment on an investment like this, it would generally carry itself. As a result, we did not think it was a silly economic excursion. We thought it made some sense. Both of us worked on weekends and in the evenings to try to make things go. As well, we had to pay the city taxes for the facility out of our own pocket, because there just was not enough cash flow in it.
We bought the place with a 10 per cent interest rate. Shortly thereafter, we found that inflation had risen to 13.5 per cent. Also, we found that interest rates were being used in an attempt to bring inflation rates down. Interest rates caused themselves to take off. Interest rates on our property rose to 20 and 22 per cent. We

could no longer afford it. In fact, it was going to break us if we hung on to it, therefore we had to dump it.

Mr. Speaker, in part, I agree with the hon. member for Regina-Wascana.
Certainly interest rates and inflation are related, but the relationship is not simply in one direction. Inflation does not simply cause high interest rates. If that were the only cause, then the hon. member would not be able to account for the increasing spread of real interest rates.
The hon. member and I can remember when there were things like 6 and 7 per cent mortgages. The difference between the inflation rate and the interest rate was usually about 1 or 2 per cent. Now, it is 4, 5, 6 and 7 per cent.
It is 10 per cent.

Somebody says it is 10 per cent. In other words, the gap between the inflation rate and the interest rate is not a clean take, but a pure take. It is a simple take by the money lenders. That benefits the kind of person who is able to pick up the property that the hon. member and his wife had to drop. I think people who have had the experience that the hon. member recounts ought to consider that a interest rate of only 1 or 2 per cent above the rate of inflation is much healthier for most people in the
country than the kind of rate that the government is promoting at present.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would clarify to which of the three Etobicoke members he was referring.
Mr. Speaker, it is the hon. member who is chairman of the finance committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to rise in support of our government's continuing commitment to provide affordable housing. All too often I have heard misguided criticism of the government's efforts in the area of housing. I would like to take this opportunity to ensure that all hon. members are aware of the significant advances made in the delivery of social resources over the past few years.
Over all, Canada is a well housed nation. The quality of our housing stock is generally high and our home ownership rate is among the highest in the world. The housing market is working well in most areas of the country, although we recognize that actions need to be taken to promote more affordable housing. I maintain that this government is providing support in this area. This is a seemingly endless task.
I had occasion to visit Europe not too very long ago and while visiting Berlin, the downtown core of a fairly large city, I found that individual home ownership was a hopeless dream, if in fact a dream at all. As a matter of fact, the people we stayed with occupied an apartment in downtown Berlin, or at least the periphery to the core, and they told us that in order to acquire this apartment they had to virtually inherit it from the previous person. I was somewhat concerned with the condition of the apartment in that it seemed as though there were certain things that had to be maintained to make it acceptable to what I thought would be the standards that these people would accept. They said that they took this apartment "as is" from the deceased person's estate in a rental situation, and if they wanted any improvements to the property, they had to provide them themselves. I think

June 6, 1990
Supply
we take for granted something the major populations of Europe to whose standards we sometimes compare ours have long since forgotten.
However, there is one segment of our population who require assistance and we are going to give it to them as best we can. They require assistance in meeting their every day housing needs. Those are the households around the core housing areas, our seniors, the disabled, single parent households, low income families, and singles, generally. There are the native people living in difficult situations in Canada's north and the urban dwellers attempting to struggle with the cost of living in high cost urban environments.
As a member of Parliament, I have had a number of opportunities to visit with and discuss the most pressing issues of the day with a number of citizens over the past few years. Of particular significance in these discussions was the desire of our constituents for equitable social programs and policies and assurance that long term planning will continue to make Canada a well housed nation. Housing programs and initiatives introduced by this government have gone a long way in achieving this end.
More specifically, actions on the part of my colleague, the hon. Minister of State for Housing, and his predecessors have resulted in a number of bold, new housing initiatives introduced in the 1980s with many more areas of progress identified for the 1990s. These areas of innovation and change have resulted in housing dollars being more finely targeted to households in need, created a new sense of partnership between all players in the housing arena, and introduced a renewed commitment to social justice and social housing policies. It is for these reasons that I stand today in response to opposition criticism of the Main Estimates for housing.
With regard to the equitable targeting of federal housing resources, it was clear to all who assumed responsibility for the housing portfolio in 1984 that major changes were required to ensure that the best possible use of social housing dollars was occurring.
After extensive review and consultation, a number of significant housing policy changes were introduced to the federal Parliament which resulted in a more equitable
distribution of federal housing dollars to those households truly in housing need. These households, including the poor, the elderly and the disabled, are the clear housing priority of our federal government.
These consultations involved all of the interest groups in the field of housing, as well as all levels of government. There was broad support at that time that housing assistance should be targeted to the most needy in our society, those who were unable to help themselves. When housing dollars are limited as a result of the current federal deficit we are faced with, our debt situation, many Canadians are opposed to the federal government spending tax dollars on housing that is not fully targeted to the most needy.
The federal government has adhered to a number of basic principles in the development of social housing policies in the 1990s. These include social housing allocations being directed to clients in core housing need and, second, all client groups in the country must have equal access to federal assistance. This ensures that citizens of our far north and rural areas are equitably served.
In conjunction with these principles, the federal government has developed a mix of programs which effectively address all types and forms of housing needs in the country. Families with affordability problems, the disabled, the disabled who may require wheelchair access, all can find housing relief in the federal group of programs.
This government has taken a number of decisive actions to ensure that inefficiencies of past programs are not repeated nor interfere with the equitable targeting and delivery of social housing resources.
Having discussed the importance of effective targeting of our housing resources, I would like to say a few words briefly concerning the manner in which the government has proceeded to involve all players in the housing field in the consultation and delivery process, and of how this process has resulted in maximizing the number of households receiving assistance under the federal group of programs.
In 1986 the government entered into agreements with the provinces and territories to jointly fund, plan, deliver


and administer housing programs. These agreements have resulted in thousands of more units being delivered to needy households through cost-sharing forumulae and a reduction in the administrative duplication from competing social housing delivery networks. This means thousands more low-income families with a solid roof over their heads and thousands more children with a warm place to sleep at night.
In recognition of the specific needs of Canada's native peoples, the federal government has designed programs which involve native peoples in all aspects of the programs. Native organizations perform an important function in the delivery of rural social housing programs in that they provide a fee-for-service delivery for the programs. This feature of the rural programs ensures that the native population is directly involved in the determination of housing program planning and delivery in each of the provinces and territories.
But we cannot solely depend on the federal government alone to solve all the problems. Housing is complex, and shared objectives and co-ordinated actions are required.
Recently, my colleague the hon. Minister of State for Housing, initiated a series of local committees which consist of the federal, provincial and local governments to address problems of housing affordability at the local level. These committees, in a number of cities from coast to coast, are dealing with impediments to the supply of affordable housing in their own communities, ranging from land availability and servicing to development approvals, all of which should assist in keeping a lid on housing costs and allow for effective use of housing dollars.
Having been associated with a municipality, I have another observation that causes me to express tonight the hope that municipalities will recognize the ongoing need for inner-city housing. While we encourage them to make the necessary zoning changes to accommodate those needs, if required, I would like to encourage them this evening to recognize this long term need and ensure that they provide long term residential zoning to maintain the residential integrity of our city cores. All to often while a plan of this kind might come in place, it seems that with the increased value of downtown proper-
Supply
ties, we find that housing stock falls to the wrecker's ball and some office building is located in its stead.
If the cities were to recognize this long-term need, it would serve their cities well and would serve to protect the necessary social infrastructure that is required to be put in place to maintain these inner-city developments.
Co-operative and non-profit organizations, our third sector, are another major group which our government looks to in the area of housing. For many years, the vital component of the Canadian housing scene has been a principal actor in using federal funds to provide services to needy households. In recognition of this role, the government recently increased the fee schedule for resource groups in the third sector to ensure necessary financial returns for their work. I believe that with this initiative, these groups can continue to effectively contribute to the housing of the nation. With their knowledge of housing development and management, they have already been involved in work on non-profit co-op housing, in many areas across our country.
Up until this time, I have been focusing on the partnerships this government has built with other governments and third sector housing organizations. But first and foremost are the individuals to whom housing solutions are addressed. Our government is committed to the involvement of each and every citizen of the country in the determination of how their shelter needs will be addressed. In this regard, for example, regional forums are being conducted to allow for input by seniors into the development of future programs specifically designed to meet their housing needs. This government can be extremely proud of its record of open consultation on housing policies since 1985, much to the benefit of households across this land.
Another area of note in the ongoing consultation of this government with the citizens of Canada is the residential participation initiative for clients residing in our public housing stock. Every person seeks the opportunity to influence their environment, including their particular housing situation. No one wants to sit passively by while others shape their surroundings. This is as true for people living in public housing as for anyone. For low-income families, it is often doubly important that they have the scope to enhance their skills so that

June 6, 1990
Supply
they may reach beyond their circumstances and play a fuller role in the broader community.
The interest expressed by public housing tenants in becoming involved in the day-to-day operations of their housing was identified in a public housing evaluation conducted by CMHC. The hon. Minister of State for Housing recently announced a set of initiatives aimed at expanding the opportunities public housing residents have to get involved, to contribute in their own way to improving and maintaining their quality of life.
The mention of community involvement brings me to my last area of comment, and that is the importance of achieving a sense of social justice with all our social programs, including housing. It is in this regard that current housing initiatives are providing a cornerstone to our future.
Approval of housing budgets by this Parliament will allow for the further development of a number of important initiatives which affect the quality of life of a great many Canadians into the 21st century. Included in this package are policies and potential housing program designs which more effectively address senior citizens, single parents and native client group needs. In addition, research efforts are continuing on a number of fronts pertaining to housing and the environment, an important area that must be given immediate priority.
One example of forward planning and research is the ongoing investigation of indoor air quality, perhaps something we could use in this House of Commons. However, CMHC not being involved with the House of Commons as its area of jurisdiction, as you well know, has a long record of involvement in the particular area of indoor air quality in residential housing stocks. I thought I had better make that clear.
In recent years, investigations have focused on specific pollutants such as methane and radon gas which enter basements from the soil. The primary focus has been on finding ways to protect housing from hazards in the soil and ensuring that remedial measures do not adversely affect other aspects of the housing unit. Performance research of this nature must continue if we are to be able to assure our children of safe, secure living environments in the future.
I would ask Parliament's support in the approval of the plans for this government to implement its much needed housing policies. As mentioned earlier, current programs and delivery practices have been significantly improved from the early 1980s with a very clear focus being given to households experiencing the most severe housing needs.
In addition, an efficient and effective federal-provincial delivery network has been developed to allocate and manage our scarce resources. Housing funding for the 1990 period will also allow for the innovative work to continue to ensure our housing future into the 1990s and into the next century.
