Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with great care to the speakers on the government side for the last couple of hours defend their policy. In defence of the government policy on housing, they miss the point. The point is that since 1984 the federal government has totally withdrawn from urban Canada. That can be measured in many ways. Perhaps we could attack directly the role of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation because it is the signal to every Canadian that the government no longer cares about the price of their housing, the suitability of their accommodation or the availability of different types of housing stock.
I would like to speak directly about one particular city, Winnipeg, which is having a great deal of difficulty in dealing with the housing crisis as a result of the withdrawal of the federal government.
A lot of people look at the prices of houses in Winnipeg and say "You are very lucky to be from Winnipeg because it is one of the most affordable housing cities in this country". On the contrary, that is an illusion because the quality of the housing stock has dropped dramatically in that the federal government is no longer involved in programs.
For example, in Winnipeg North Centre, four out of ten families live below the poverty level, which is double the rate for the rest of the city. Within this context, at one time the federal government provided a great deal of housing through RRAP and the neighbourhood improvement program in the 1970s, and the infrastructure was built.
June 6, 1990

One of the neighbourhoods, North Point Douglas, was the most accomplished example of urban reform in North America. When Canadian government officials went elsewhere to talk about housing projects, they always pointed to North Point Douglas in Winnipeg as an example of how the three levels of governments could work together.
As a follow-up to the neighbourhood improvement programs, in 1980 Winnipeg entered the core area initiative with the two levels of government, again with this commitment to urban renewal.
I raise this in the context of the housing programs because when you are trying to do urban renewal you are trying to stabilize in part the housing structure. You are not only concerned with the construction of newer houses, which is very important for low-income families, for disabled persons and for the elderly, but you also have to take a look at the existing housing stock.
In cities again such as Winnipeg and Winnipeg North Centre where most people are renters, the quality of the house is not only dependent upon their own efforts, but also dependent upon the efforts of the landlords. Winnipeg used rental RRAP more extensively than any other city in the country.

And Montreal. Of course those are the two cities which stood up to the government and asked that that program be continued. The silence of the minister on that issue last year is well remembered. Toronto has another set of problems. We are asking you to deal with the problems of Winnipeg tonight.
As the minister has taken an interest in this point, he will know that rental RRAP was very successful in downtown Winnipeg.
As Winnipeg housing stock continues to age, the fact that renewal has not taken place, the fact that there are no market dynamics which cause people to invest in housing in a substantial way, and the fact that there is no access to programming make it even more difficult for families and individuals to begin to redevelop those houses.
The reason this debate comes at a very crucial time is that the core area initiative, the second phase of it, is coming to a close next year. There have been no measures put on the table by the federal government to

renew that. Not only do we have Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation on its own withdrawing from the city of Winnipeg, we now find that the federal government as a group-all the ministries whether it is employment, transport or the ERDA agreements-is withdrawing its support for the older neighbourhoods in Winnipeg.
As a result, people who are working in housing projects in North Winnipeg, those who are trying to see what they can do about North Point Douglas, those who are looking at the question of the homeless or North Main, and those who are trying to figure out ways of repairing homes in the Woolsley area are turning to their political leaders at all three levels of government and asking: "Why aren't you helping us this time?" Each level of government is turning to the other looking for a signal of support, looking for somebody who will stand up and say: "All right, let's begin to reconstruct these neighbourhoods".
It is a total package to make a neighbourhood work. It requires improved policing and streets. It requires the city to spend a lot of money on infrastructure. It requires the provincial government to make sure that its programming in areas such as welfare are in proper condition. It is also requires the federal government to step forward with the needed capital so that the individual units are also in good shape.
Of particular concern in downtown Winnipeg is the plight of our many aboriginal peoples. It is estimated that within my constituency alone there are more than 20,000 aboriginal people. One of the areas that this government has cut back the greatest amount of money is moneys available for aboriginal groups to develop housing projects in an urban environment. Because of that these groups are unable either to access capital, expertise, or land. None of the components needed for housing projects are available to them.
As the quality of housing and rental units continues to decline because of rental RRAP no longer being available, and as individual families because of lack of jobs cannot buy their own homes and begin to fix them up, the cycle of decline has been accentuated. People are turning to the government right now and saying: "Give us some hope. Give us some reason to expect that in the next couple of years we will see a renewal of the core

area initiative in Winnipeg and a redevelopment of our neighbourhoods".
Winnipeg in this respect is the best image for understanding the decline of urban Canada as affected by housing policy. In one extreme, a city like Toronto, where affordable housing escapes middle class and working class families-
Or is non-existent.

"Or is non-existent", as a member from Toronto properly points out. Then Winnipeg is the opposite extreme on the continuum, having absolutely no access to capital to renovate those homes and rebuild the neighbourhoods.
We have asked the government to listen to these points today and to consider that it has a proper role. speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:

here tonight in the truly objective way in which you would want me to, of course.

I do not think any member on this side sees any willingness on the part of the government to look after people. I look forward to seeing a change.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively tonight as we started with the Minister of State for Housing. He made remarks on how he has travelled across the country and listened to single parents, natives, young couples, and seniors. He recognized that there are difficulties. As I listened to his speech I got the feeling that he did not really understand that it is one thing to listen to these people but what are we going to do about the crisis that we are involved with right now in housing?
The member knows that there is a crisis because if you come from Toronto you cannot help but feel the pain, the frustration and the worry. In the city of Toronto today the price for an average home is around $275,000. Young people today are almost ready to throw away the thought of ever owning a home. We do not measure the social costs of this frustration that is building up within our community.
Our caucus, led by the member for London East, met with the Toronto Home Builders Association because we knew we would be having this debate in the House tonight and we wanted to speak directly to those in the community who were involved directly with the home building situation. We can listen to just our own constitu-

Supply
ents but then we get a view from only one particular part of the community.
We met today with the leaders of that industry. The fact of the matter is that the housing industry in the greater metropolitan Toronto area has almost totally collapsed. One of the most revealing facts we heard from them today was that Canada Mortgage and Housing statistics are about six to eight months behind. The minister talked about a projection of 200,000 units, but these senior officials today from the Toronto Home Builders Association said that it was more like 100,000.
We know that the Governor of the Bank of Canada bases his interest rate policy on numbers he gets from various departments of government, including Statistics Canada and Canada Mortgage and Housing, from which he develops his models. So the whole premise upon which this government is setting its interest rates is based upon a false set of numbers.
The next thing we know, the Governor of the Bank of Canada is saying that the problem is not as bad as we on this side of the House are saying, so the government continues with its financial plan and the Governor continues with his. In the meantime, something different is really happening.
Right now the situation in the city of Toronto is such that 75 per cent of the people in the home building industry, trades and sub-trades, have not hired any new employees in the last six months. In fact, almost 90 per cent of these people are laying off. They said to us today that the housing crisis is far worse today than it was in 1981-82.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this will not affect only the home building industry. This will ultimately affect the furniture industry and have a chain effect all the way through the system. Every sector of our economy is affected by the home building industry.
Another affect of the crisis in Toronto today is that many of the fabulous craftsmen who are building beautiful homes go into other sectors when an industry collapses like this. They go into the service sector. When the market recovers, we no longer have those skilled craftsmen. As a result we have to retrain at a tremendous cost. That tremendous cost will again be added on to the cost of our housing.
I know that our time is short here tonight. The bottom line is that this government should not be patting itself
on the back for the current housing program that it is unveiling. I know this Minister of Housing is sincere but, as he mentioned in his speech, beyond the economic responsibility this a social responsibility to which we have to attend. This minister has to go back to his cabinet colleagues and be a lot more forceful in terms of his requirements.
The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not meant to be a passive operator. Right now it is virtually an organization in mothballs. It needs to be taken out of mothballs. It needs to be much more aggressive. The minister said in his speech that there are municipalities where single by-laws are holding up some of the good intentions and goodwill that he wants to put forward. The national government has many instruments to activate municipalities to move more quickly if the national will of this government is to make sure that affordable housing is available.
Another problem that we have in this country, especially in the greater metropolitan area, is the lack of serviced land. We need to give our municipalities much more help in terms of infrastructure so that serviced land is made available.
I do not shy away from the responsibility of deficit and debt, but at the same time, having people out of work is going to put a tremendous strain on the support systems of this government. That is not going to allow it to keep to its financial plan. The Minister of Housing knows that the best way to get the financial plan of this government in order is to make sure that everybody is working, and he should start with the housing industry.
The Minister of Finance talked today about unit labour costs. His theme this week is unit labour costs. He is really worried about the fact that our unit labour costs are going up. Of course they are going up. If there is no sense of fairness, if one does not get a sense that the job is going to be there for a long time, productivity falls off. The Minister of Finance has stopped listening to the grassroots people in this country. He is not only listening to the technocrats in his own department, he is following those models that are being built in the office of the Governor of the Bank of Canada which are 20 years outdated.
They say that there is not a problem in Toronto. I can tell you that there are bankers who are scared silly because of people who are walking away from deposits on homes. Some are walking away from deposits of as much as $40,000 and $50,000. If we do not put a tighter
June 6, 1990

focus on this housing crisis, we are going to lose two or three trust companies.
I am not suggesting for a minute that this is an easy problem to solve. However, I am suggesting that this is a problem that needs almost as much attention as we are putting into the other problem being discussed over at the Conference Centre tonight. We should make sure that we never let this issue be taken off the front burner until we get our interest rates back down to around 11 per cent, so that we can make sure that we have affordable housing and full time jobs are back again.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most interested in the hon. member's comments with respect to the home building industry and his meeting today with its representatives. I was most interested as well in his comments with respect to interest rates.
Recently a writer in The Toronto Star-a. newspaper which I am sure the hon. member reads on a regular basis-Mr. Warren Potter, had some comments with respect to that. I would like to have the hon. member's comments with respect to Mr. Potter's thoughts on the issue. He said:
It's easy to guess why serious buyers are holding back. They use the high mortgage interest rates as a rationale, but they are really hoping that the falling house prices will tumble even further.
Builders are crying the blues, but some of them have only themselves to blame.
They've misjudged the market. They've kept on building these monster homes for the Yuppies.
The builders who are really hurting are those who, like the sellers of resale homes, refused to believe that the housing boom would end.
I wonder if the hon. member has some thoughts and comments with respect to that point of view on the housing situation.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to tell the hon. minister that I do not read The Toronto Star regularly. I am not familiar with the specific article to which he refers, but I think that Warren Potter is correct to the extent that the province and the municipalities have made a mistake in the plan of subdivisions they
Supply
have been approving in the last three or four years in the greater metropolitan Toronto area.
When I drive up Bayview Avenue in Richmond Hill just south of the Aurora area I see homes that cost $700,000 or $800,000 and yet I hear of projects like Queensville Properties north of Queensville where they are trying to produce close to 5,000 affordable units at $150,000 apiece but are having problems getting their sewage allocation and zoning. I think there is something wrong with that.
My point is that the national government, with its levers, its resources and its access to various instruments, should come in and correct those situations. It can control the cash to the provinces and to the municipalities. It can use all those instruments. That is how Canada Mortgage and Housing came into being.
I have no problem with cutting back on some of those $700,000 and $800,000 units in Toronto because they are not serving anyone.

Mr. Speaker, this may be the single most important debate that the people in Canada who are watching this debate this evening and thinking of purchasing a home will view this year and for years to come.
I want to compliment my friend and colleague from London East who moved the motion today in order that we could get into a debate on the vital area of housing and the crisis of housing in Canada.
I looked several times towards the Chair as members on this side of the House were speaking, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure that you were as impressed as I was with the wealth of knowledge and depth of information that the member for Winnipeg North Centre and the member for Broadview-Greenwood have on this vital issue and the crisis in which we find ourselves in the housing situation and the housing industry in Canada today. I am sure that after my short intervention you will be as impressed with our member for Eglinton-Lawrence who has some very important words on this issue.
We have heard a lot about the problems that have faced our housing industry since 1984.1 want to reiterate some of the things I have heard in this House since this debate began which really show the crisis we face. One point three million Canadians are paying well over 30 per cent of their combined incomes for shelter. As you know,

June 6, 1990
Supply
30 per cent is the maximum they should be paying and they are paying 40 per cent, 50 per cent and sometimes 60 per cent just to provide shelter for themselves and their families.
Forty per cent of single parents are living in accommodation which is below the minimum standards acceptable in the country.
We have talked about caring for our seniors. Forty per cent of our single seniors spend their final years spending in excess of 50 per cent of their income just for accommodation.
In Ontario alone, as the member for Broadwood- Greenwood stated, 54,000 families in Ontario are waiting to find some form of affordable housing. Today, with the economy that the government has created, the interest rate is soaring to such a rate that the rate on a one-year mortgage exceeds 15 per cent. That takes so many people out of the market. Their dream of owning a home has to be set aside for the next few years until the Liberals take power and bring in a more acceptable program for affordable housing so that our young people can afford to realize their national dream.
Those are just some of the issues that I am sure you are interested in hearing, Mr. Speaker. I wish I had more time to expand on them.
Let me close my few remarks by talking about what I consider to be the national dream for all young Canadian families, young couples who are married with children. Their dream is to own a home. In the economy that has been created by the government since 1984, there is not a chance that they can own a home, given that the average three-bedroom bungalow now costs about $140,000 and interest rates exceed 15 per cent. When most of us buy a home, we have to mortgage it. The payments far exceed that young couple's combined income.
Your generation and mine, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps some of the other generations in the House, have created an economy that requires two incomes in order to purchase a home. This government has failed to provide proper daycare services to enable both husband and wife to go out to work so that they can afford a home.
These are the issues that are facing our country today that are so vital to young married couples in our
communities with young children who require, not a home, but basic shelter so that they can live in comfort and dignity, as all Canadians should, and realize their Canadian dream. It is the actions of the government that are depriving them of this dream.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most interested to hear the hon. member's comments with respect to the way his party hopes that it would have the opportunity to manage the economy in the coming years.
I think back to the days prior to the 1984 election and the inspiration that brought me to run for office federally. I remember, for instance, under the former Liberal government, astronomical inflation shooting through the roof, followed by astronomical interest rates with mortgage interest rates reaching 23 per cent. This was followed by devastating bankruptcies and double digit unemployment. That is compared to the unemployment rate that we have today which is very low, one of the lowest in years.
Is this the kind of management of the economy that the hon. member would like to bring back to the country?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. minister's question. It really zeroes in on exactly what I said earlier in my remarks.
What the hon. minister was talking about in the early 1980s was a world economy. What was happening in Canada was being paralleled in every other country in the world. Canada was not alone. The United States was experiencing the inflationary trend and the high interest trend. England was going through the same type of economic revolution. Every free country in the world was going through the same situation.
The difference today, in answer to my friend, is that Canada is going through this terrible period of high inflation, high prices, and high interest rates, but our friends in other parts of the world are not experiencing this. That is the big difference. That is where the mismanagement of this economy comes in.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to add my voice to those of my hon. colleagues who have spoken most eloquently about the deficiency in the housing market in Canada, and most especially in the Toronto area.
June 6, 1990

I want to compliment my colleague from Broadview- Greenwood who highlighted a very serious problem in the city of Toronto and southern Ontario.
It is no wonder that the problem is as serious as it is when we look at the government's record of cutbacks in CMHC and funds available for the stimulation and development of the housing market. We have inventory of some 200,000 first-time buyers in Canada. In Ontario, we have a prediction of only 52,000 new homes for this year when the Treasurer of Ontario had predicted at least 29,000 more.
This is a very serious problem, most especially in the Toronto area. When one looks at some of the figures and the incomes, one is tempted to say that this is fat-cat city, that people are well-off, and that there is not a problem. However, in Toronto, the average mortgage and taxes for a typical family amount to some $31,829 per annum, when the Canadian average is only somewhere around $17,500. In Toronto, the average percentage of income for financing a house is 49.8 this year, compared to the Canadian average of 35.3 per cent. In 1981, in Toronto that percentage was only 33.1. There has been an increase of well over 15 per cent. In Canada, that average has been maintained at about 34 per cent.
The average family in Toronto can only afford a house in the vicinity of $159,000, yet the average price is well over $100,000 more than that. There are over 500,000 tenant households in metro Toronto, with 372,000 of them considered potential first-time buyers. Yet, there will be 29,000 fewer new homes than predicted by the Treasurer of Ontario.
There is a dual problem with that. The dual problem is that the lethargy in the construction industry has spinoffs, all of them negative, for what is happening in industry as whole.
Of Ontario's workforce, 12 per cent, or some 552,000 men and women, in 1989 were employed in the construction industry. That industry is expected to grow by only 1.3 per cent in this coming year. That is well below the growth rate of all other industries. In the Toronto area,
35,000	workers, as my colleague pointed out, have lost their jobs and many more will join them. This is 35,000 in the construction industry, in skilled trades, where the average salary is somewhere between $25 and $29 per hour.
Supply
I know that the minister will agree with me that the big problem stems from the government's financial and interest rates policies. In fact, every increase of 1 per cent in interest rates between 9 and 14 per cent-and we are well in that range-eliminates 100,000 potential first-time home buyers. Every increase of one per cent in interest rates decreases the construction industry's output by 2.5 to 3 per cent and results in the loss of some
40,000	jobs. We are well in that range already.
This government has got to change its policies.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that my time is short, but I am pleased to address this House tonight on a matter which concerns a large number of our fellow Canadians who look to their government for help.
I refer to the individuals, families, and seniors in search of affordable housing: people who look to their government for what most of us in this House take for granted, people who like all of us aspire to live decently and in dignity, people who without help will need to make untold sacrifices so that their children do not go without a roof over their heads, people who without help may not even be able to make these sacrifices and will go without a place they can call their home.
Every day this House hears about the need to assist this industry, that province, or this other town. Every day this government explains how the competing needs of the people of this land are weighted and the strategies that are in place. In many ways there are several analogies to be made between the single mother seeking a decent home for her children and the person who lost a job, between the senior facing rising rents and a low income worker unable to make ends meet. The common thread between these people is the need for a caring government.
My colleagues and I feel for these people. We feel a need to reach out to them and we do, but not to the extent we would like to. This is when we become angry because with all the resources that this country should be able to draw on to help those experiencing hard times, the government of all Canadians must at the same time practise fiscal restraint because the legacy of the previous government has been a series of ill-conceived programs and unpaid expenditures.

June 6, 1990
Supply
The government reaches out but must play the delicate balancing act between competing demands on the public purse. This is responsible government, the type of government which if it had been in place earlier would have avoided the financial mess bequeathed by over two decades of mismanagement.
When I watched the proceedings of the Charest Commission I was touched by the words of Mr. Jim Sinclair when he recalled his childhood as a Metis in Saskatchewan living in a barracks. He touched the fibre of what being a Canadian means to most of us. What Mr. Sinclair related meant more to me than any of the learned dissertations about the constitutional basis for the use of federal spending powers. When he spoke I understood that the powers were not only rooted in the law of the land but also in his heart and the country's heart. When he spoke I told myself that neither he nor his children should again experience the violence of poverty and that Canada should continue to offer the type of housing programs which offer the poor and less fortunate among us a chance to live in dignity and to become productive citizens.
The measures that this government has taken since my colleague the present Minister of National Defence stood in this House late in 1985 were and continue to be measures to serve those who need the government's help most.

Madam Speaker, I think this is the first time in the history of Parliament that we have obtained something, which I wish to point out to my colleagues, especially those whose language is French. I see big smiles on those who do not know exactly what I am going to say. I think that we should congratulate the Clerk and the House for having kindly agreed to a proposal that I have been making for years and that I repeated twice publicly: finally in the appendix we have "Alphabetical" in English on one side and "Alphabeti-que" in French on the other for items in alphabetical order. That was never done before. We had been told
June 6, 1990

that it was totally impossible. And for those who want to follow, and some here may be interested in following what happens occasionally, we finally have a working document that makes sense and is understandable. The only suggestion I would make is that the items under each heading could also be in alphabetical order. But I want to say that for the first time we can work in either language.
